Last week, Sheinbaum traveled to Shenzhen, China, for the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, flying economy alongside other passengers. The decision made waves on Chinese social media — and came up again Friday at the popular Mexican festival, where 72,000 people packed the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, according to promoter Ocesa.

In a recent development, “I f— with Mexico because you have a revolutionary spirit here,” Albarn told the crowd. “This is an inspirational country, and I don’t know too much about your president, but the fact that she traveled economy class, for me, is a really crucial… It’s a statement, you know? So, I salute you all.”.

Albarn made the comment while wearing a red beret and military-style jacket, an image that fit the occasion: Mexico’s Revolution Day, observed every Nov. 20 to mark the start of the 1910 armed uprising against Porfirio Díaz, who had been in power for more than 30 years.

Earlier in the set, Johnny Marr joined the band for “The Empty Dream Machine” and “Casablanca”; he played on the studio versions of both on Gorillaz’s The Mountain (2026). He also performed “The Plastic Guru” and “The Sweet Prince,” which also appear on the album.

It has been revealed that trueno, meanwhile, joined the collective — formed 28 years ago by Albarn, former frontman of Blur, and illustrator Jamie Hewlett — for “THE MANIFESTO,” their collaboration from The Mountain. He also freestyled during “Clint Eastwood,” the song that closed the set.

When Trueno shouted “¡Viva México, cabrones!” during “Clint Eastwood,” Albarn burst out laughing and kept singing offbeat as he tried to hold it together. Trueno also used the stage to hype up his favorite soccer team, Club Atlético Boca Juniors, proudly wearing the club’s blue-and-gold jersey.

In a recent development, mexican singer Luisa Almaguer was another special guest, joining Gorillaz for “Latin Simone (¿Qué Pasa Contigo?),” the 2001 song originally sung by the late Cuban star Ibrahim Ferrer for the band’s self-titled debut album. Her appearance made for an emotional moment with the crowd. Almaguer previously took part in Albarn’s Africa Express project and was chosen to open Gorillaz’s Latin American tour in November and December.

In a recent development, the British collective also welcomed singer Kara Jackson for “Orange County,” U.S. rapper Bootie Brown for “Dirty Harry” and “Stylo,” and MC Black Thought for “The Sad God.”.

Alongside Gorillaz, other acts performing on the first day of Corona Capital included James Blake, Mumford & Sons, CHVRCHES, Yung Lean, The Kooks, Violet Grohl, Jamie xx, Durand Jones & The Indications, CMAT and Grace Ives.

The festival’s second day, Saturday (Nov. 21), is set to feature Twenty One Pilots, The Offspring, Pierce the Veil, Underworld, Sébastien Tellier and Peaches, among others.

In a recent development, germany, who finished top of Group A2 following their 5-0 win over the Netherlands in Berlin on Monday are to face Belgium in the Nations League quarterfinals — after they finished second in Group A1. The Belgians recently came up with a statement result of their own, beating Italy 4-1. The match-up between the neighboring countries promises to be closely contested, with Belgium sitting at No. 8 in the men's rankings, three places above Germany.

The head coach of Belgium is former Bayern Munich player Mark van Bommel, who took over from Rudi Garcia following the World Cup, where they were knocked out by eventual champions Spain in the quarterfinals.

Germany head into the knockout phase on a high note, not only because they won their group, but also the way they performed in their last two matches, against Serbia and the Netherlands in the group stage.

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp followed the draw, held in Nyon on Friday, from the German FA's (DFB) Frankfurt offices. He played down the notion that Germany enter the tie as the favorites.

Recent findings suggest that "I've practically never given it any thought. It's never interested me," he noted.

Recent findings suggest that "An awful lot can happen in that time. We're very happy with the final impression we left, yet we're also fully aware that we're only at the very beginning of a development process. We want to carry this positive momentum forward—there's still a great deal to be done.".

The matches are slated for March 25 and March 30, 2027, and having won their group, Germany will have home-field advantage for the second leg.

Germany and Belgium have faced each other 26 times to date, with West Germany and Germany having the upper hand with 20 wins, five defeats and one draw.

Should Germany advance to the semifinals, they will go on to face the winner of England and Norway, a World Cup quarterfinals rematch.

In the other two semifinals matchups, the Netherlands drew Portugal, while the top pairing sees Spain face France in a rematch of one of last summer's World Cup semifinals.

The "Final Four" mini tournament is to be held from June 9 to 13 but the host venue won't be determined until the semifinal lineup has been completed.

#59200. A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study

A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1475 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, an existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for newly introduced treatments for chronic neck and back pain.
  • The discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine.
  • It has been revealed that although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer latest ways to slow spinal degeneration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, an existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for newly introduced treatments for chronic neck and back pain. In experiments involving zebrafish, researchers found that the medication prevented abnormal mineral deposits from forming in the spine, a process that can cause spinal tissues to harden and vertebrae to fuse together.

The discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine. Researchers also identified changes in gene activity and metabolism that appear to contribute to this damage, revealing several possible targets for future treatments.

It has been revealed that although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer latest ways to slow spinal degeneration. The research also demonstrates how zebrafish could help scientists investigate the causes of spinal disease and test potential therapies.

In a recent development, most people experience back pain at some point in their lives, and one common cause is the deterioration of the spine's natural shock absorbers. These structures, called intervertebral discs, sit between the vertebrae and help the spine absorb pressure, distribute weight, and move comfortably.

According to recent reports, over time, the discs can lose their ability to cushion the spine, a condition known as intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). As the discs deteriorate, they can contribute to pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility.

Despite the widespread impact and substantial economic burden of this condition, no medications are right now available that can stop or reverse the degenerative process. Surgery remains the only established long-term intervention for certain severe cases, creating an urgent need for treatments that address the underlying damage.

Researchers have long known that genetics influences the risk of developing spinal disc degeneration. One gene of particular interest is associated with collagen IX, a protein that helps maintain the structural integrity of spinal discs by supporting the network of fibers that holds them together. Variations affecting this gene have repeatedly been associated with disc problems that develop earlier in life.

To investigate how these genetic changes contribute to spinal damage, scientists at the Universities of Edinburgh and Bristol turned to zebrafish. They studied fish that had been bred without a functioning copy of the gene, allowing them to observe how its absence affected the spine as the animals grew older.

A Hidden Process Causes the Spine To Harden.

The results revealed striking similarities between the genetically altered zebrafish and people with degenerative spinal disease.

As the fish aged, abnormal mineral deposits accumulated in the tissues separating their vertebrae. This process, known as mineralization, involves minerals collecting in tissues where they do not normally belong. In the spine, the buildup can cause normally flexible structures to become unusually rigid, much like unwanted bone forming in the wrong location.

The researchers also observed spinal fusion, in which neighboring vertebrae become joined together. Such changes can interfere with the spine's normal flexibility and movement.

In a recent development, importantly, the scientists discovered that the damage began well before the mineral deposits appeared. An underlying layer that provides structural support during spinal development started to break down first, suggesting that deterioration of this protective framework may set the stage for later hardening.

This finding could help explain how genetic changes initiate a chain reaction that eventually damages the spine.

Surprising Links to Fat Metabolism and Vitamin A.

According to recent reports, to understand what was happening at the molecular level, the team examined patterns of gene activity in the zebrafish. This allowed them to identify biological processes that had become unusually active or disrupted as spinal degeneration developed.

Several unexpected connections emerged.

It has been revealed that the researchers found alterations in fat metabolism, the processes through which the body breaks down, stores, and uses fats. They also detected disturbances in a cellular signaling system called mTOR, which helps regulate cell growth, metabolism, and responses to nutrients.

Additional changes involved phosphate regulation and vitamin A signaling. Phosphate is an essential mineral involved in building bones and teeth, but its accumulation in the wrong tissues can contribute to abnormal hardening. Vitamin A signaling helps control how cells develop and function.

Industry observers note that together, these findings suggest that spinal disc degeneration involves more than the gradual wearing down of tissues. Changes in how cells process nutrients, regulate growth, and handle minerals may also play crucial roles.

An Osteoporosis Drug Blocks Spinal Mineral Buildup.

One of the most promising discoveries came when researchers tested ways to reduce the spinal abnormalities.

A medication belonging to a class of drugs called bisphosphonates successfully blocked the abnormal mineral buildup in the zebrafish. Bisphosphonates are already used to treat osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures. These medications help protect bones by slowing the processes that break down bone tissue.

The finding is especially intriguing because it suggests that a treatment already used in patients might also help researchers develop therapies for spinal degeneration.

The team identified other approaches that reduced spinal damage. Limiting how much food the zebrafish consumed led to fewer spinal fusions, as did medications that suppressed fat metabolism.

These results point toward fat metabolism and phosphate regulation as potentially important targets for future drugs.

However, the experiments were conducted in zebrafish, not humans. More research will be needed to determine whether the same biological mechanisms operate in people and whether targeting them can safely prevent or slow spinal disc degeneration. The dietary findings also do not establish that restricting food intake can prevent spinal damage in humans.

Fresh Hope for Chronic Back Pain Treatments.

The study was published in the journal Communications Biology and received support from Arthritis UK and BBSRC.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Erika Kague, who led the research at the University of Edinburgh's Institute of Genetics and Cancer, emphasized the potential significance of identifying treatments that target the underlying causes of spinal damage.

"For decades, surgery has been the only real answer for disc disease. By understanding the biology that drives the spine to harden, our zebrafish studies point to several ways of slowing it down, including a drug already used safely in patients. There's more work to do, but for a condition that's affected people for generations without a treatment in sight, this is super exciting.".

The findings could be particularly important for the millions of people who live with persistent back pain and have limited options for preventing their condition from worsening.

Dr. Caroline Aylott, Head of Research Delivery at Arthritis UK, highlighted the potential benefits for patients.

"For the 9.5 million people across the UK living with back pain this research brings fresh hope that potential new therapeutic approaches are on the horizon.

"We are proud to fund research that is unlocking the science behind the processes leading to spinal disc degeneration. Back pain is one of the UK's most common conditions that has blighted millions over generations. Dr. Erika Kague and her team at the University of Edinburgh have uncovered crucial genetic evidence that could pave the way for latest treatments, bringing us one step closer to a future where fewer people have to live with the daily pain and challenges that back pain can bring.".

The research also illustrates the broader value of studying basic biological processes to understand diseases that affect large numbers of people.

In a recent development, dr. Jef Grainger, Executive Director for Bioscience Advancing Knowledge at BBSRC, said:.

"This research shows how publicly funded discovery bioscience can generate the knowledge needed to address major health challenges. By revealing fresh knowledge of how healthy biological processes break down in aging-related spinal disc degeneration, the study opens up promising avenues for future treatment development. It's a great example of how BBSRC-supported research helps turn scientific discovery into knowledge and innovations that have the potential to improve people's lives.".

By identifying genetic and metabolic changes that contribute to spinal hardening, and demonstrating that some of the damage can be prevented in zebrafish, the researchers have opened several fresh avenues for investigating spinal disc degeneration.

For a condition that affects millions and has no approved drug capable of stopping its progression, these early findings offer an encouraging starting point for developing treatments that could one day protect the spine before serious damage occurs.

Voyager 1 had a data outage when it hit one light day. It still does.

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While Voyager 1 pushed past the one light-day distance milestone, the 49-year-old probe actually hadn't sent any science or engineering information home for days.
  • Voyager 1 still beams a steady radio signal to Earth, which tells engineers the spacecraft is alive and its antenna still points at Earth.
  • Voyager 1 crossed the milestone at 5:16 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While Voyager 1 pushed past the one light-day distance milestone, the 49-year-old probe actually hadn't sent any science or engineering information home for days.

The trouble started Nov. 14, and it hasn't let up. Voyager 1 still beams a steady radio signal to Earth, which tells engineers the spacecraft is alive and its antenna still points at Earth. But the signal carries no information about the probe's health or what its instruments are measuring, and engineers don't yet know why.

Voyager 1 crossed the milestone at 5:16 a.m. ET Nov. 18, about 16.1 billion miles away, according to NASA. No other human-made object has traveled so far. Because the probe's radio signal takes a full day to cross space, the team didn't get word until 5:16 a.m. ET Nov. 19, when a ground antenna near Madrid picked it up.

NASA marked the achievement Thursday with an hourlong celebration at its Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California that may have overshadowed the problem. Panelists shared memories of the mission, the agency played a video from fans around the world, and astronaut Jessica Watkins aboard the International Space Station provided a recorded tribute. The host covered the data outage in two sentences before opening the floor to questions. Officials delved into the spacecraft's current condition only after a reporter asked how the spacecraft was doing.

Recent findings suggest that "We have an anomaly that is not something unseen before," remarked Suzanne Dodd, Voyager's project manager. "We do have a very strong carrier signal. We presently don't have a frame sync, so we're not getting the science or engineering data currently.".

Recent findings suggest that the carrier signal is the basic radio wave a spacecraft sends out — the same kind of wave a radio station uses to carry music. Voyager 1 normally loads its data onto that wave in packaged blocks, called frames. Antennas on Earth have to find where each block starts before anyone can read it, and that step is called the frame sync. In other words, right now, engineers can tell the station is on the air, but all they get is dead air.

All is not lost. The signal at least highlights that the computer keeping Voyager 1 aimed at Earth is doing its job, and that the probe's antenna and transmitter still work. The trouble more likely sits in a different onboard computer, the one that collects readings from the instruments and other systems and packages them for the trip home.

In a recent development, but, clearly, fixing it won't be fast. Every command engineers send takes two days to produce an answer, the reality that comes with achieving the light-day milestone. NASA warned that finding the cause could take weeks or longer.

The team says it has seen something like this before. In 2023, Voyager 1 also sent a carrier signal with no data. Engineers traced that problem to one of its onboard computers, and NASA stated that experience is guiding their troubleshooting efforts. Engineers are also checking whether the outage connects to an episode in October, when the mission lost all contact with Voyager 1 for about 48 hours before the spacecraft reconnected on its own.

Industry observers note that if the team feared the outage might be permanent, it didn't show at Thursday's event. Panelists spent most of the hour smiling and reminiscing. When the problem came up, they treated it as routine.

In a recent development, "The anomalies have become normal for us," mentioned Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager's mission manager, who later added: "An engineer with a problem is like a dog with a bone. So we are very busy and very energized to solve these problems.".

Age makes everything harder. The original commands were sent on punch cards, Badaruddin mentioned, and the team now has to make modern equipment talk to that 1970s hardware. Power keeps shrinking, too. Both Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, run on generators that turn heat from decaying plutonium into electricity, and each probe loses about four watts a year. To save energy, engineers have shut off instruments over the years. Voyager 1 now runs just two: a magnetometer, which measures magnetic fields, and a plasma wave instrument, which picks up waves in the thin, electrically charged gas of interstellar space.

It has been revealed that this summer, engineers tried a risky move and successfully turned off three devices on Voyager 1 while replacing them with lower-power alternatives that still keep its fuel from freezing. The team expects the savings to keep the probe's instruments running until at least the 50th launch anniversary next summer.

Dodd compared the spacecraft to an aging human who takes longer to bounce back.

"All of us old people have our aches and pains, and you know sometimes it takes longer to stretch out your muscles and remember things," Dodd said. "I'm confident that it won't be too long, and it will send us data back.".

Voyager 2 remains healthy with three instruments working. NASA has remarked it expects to lose both spacecraft eventually to problems engineers can't fix. But until then, the team will keep searching for workarounds like this summer's power swap.

"We pulled a rabbit out of a hat," Badaruddin noted. "If we can find some more rabbits, we'll keep doing this.".

There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1131 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible.
  • According to recent reports, then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades.
  • This fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible. There was the Hyades, the major V-shaped cluster that forms the bull's face, with Aldebaran, noticeably brighter and more orange than the other stars, the dominant star. Every diagram reinforced the arrangement — Aldebaran was the eye of Taurus, the Hyades made the face, and in my head they became one object.

According to recent reports, then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades. I remember going outside afterward and looking again, half expecting the deception to become obvious now that I knew. It didn't. Aldebaran still looked completely at home among the other stars. The difference is hidden in the one dimension our eyes judge poorly when we look into space — depth. Aldebaran is about 65 light-years away, while the Hyades are roughly 150 light-years distant. The orange eye of Taurus is a foreground star that happens to lie almost exactly along our line of sight toward the Hyades.

This fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing. The night sky looks flat, and our brains are extremely willing to believe it. But it has incredible depth — and when you can see parts of the night sky in 3D, that's when you begin to appreciate that you're not looking at a flat map. Instead, you begin to see our cosmic neighborhood as it really is. By appreciating depth, you learn its geography.

Taurus is now easy to find from the Northern Hemisphere during the evening. Once it's dark, look east for a small, tight knot of stars — the Pleiades open cluster (M45) — and then look nearby for a much larger V-shaped arrangement. That V is the Hyades, with unmistakably orange Aldebaran apparently sitting on one arm. Aldebaran's name is derived from the Arabic Al Dabarān, meaning "the follower," because it appears to trail the Pleiades across the night sky.

The Hyades is a real physical group of stars — an open cluster — that formed together and moves through our galaxy together. About 153 light-years away, the Hyades is the nearest open star cluster to Earth. The name means "the rainmakers" because their rising and setting times in the ancient Greek sky coincided with wet weather. The stars in the Hyades are of a similar age — and mostly sun-like stars, or similar — so astronomers can tell that they all formed together in the same nebula.

Orange-red star Aldebaran — the 14th-brightest star in the night sky — is the interloper, sitting less than half as far away from the sun. If you could somehow view the neighborhood from another part of the Milky Way, the familiar arrangement would fall apart. Aldebaran would no longer sit conveniently in the bull's face, and Taurus itself would stop looking like a bull.

Industry observers note that constellations aren't objects in the same sense as a planet or star cluster. They are merely views. Even stars that appear almost side by side can be separated by enormous distances. Our entire view of the night sky is a line-of-sight, 2D phenomenon — so all the patterns we see are an illusion.

Industry observers note that start with Aldebaran and the Hyades using only unaided eyes. Once you have the V, remind yourself of the distances — roughly 65 light-years for Aldebaran and 150 for the Hyades — and try to imagine pulling the orange star toward you while leaving the rest of the cluster behind. Stargazing like this can be much harder than it sounds. Even the brains of seasoned stargazers are hard-wired to find patterns of stars — constellations — and they rarely practice seeing stars at their correct distances.

Sources indicate that binoculars are worth using for the Hyades because the cluster is broad, so low magnification suits it well. Binoculars show many additional stars, but that's not really the point. Knowing what you're looking at changes the observation more than magnification does.

According to recent reports, trying to see the night sky in 3D is best done one constellation at a time, but I warn you — it makes you suspicious of everything. Next time you trace Orion, Cassiopeia or Auriga, you'll always be wondering which stars are nearby and which merely look that way. Looking up the distances and working it all out for yourself is an eye-opening experience.

Learning constellations gets you around the sky in a basic sense, but learning how to dismantle them and put them back together is when you begin to know the night sky as it really is.

This week is dominated by the moon. The moon is already waxing when the week begins and becomes the full Beaver Moon — a supermoon — on Nov. 24. That means progressively brighter evening skies and increasingly poor conditions for faint galaxies, nebulae and other low-contrast objects. Aldebaran and the main Hyades stars are bright enough to see from suburban skies even under strong moonlight, so you don't need to travel somewhere properly dark. Swapping your view from 2D to 3D takes only a little imagination. However, that could change in the few nights around the full moon — particularly on Nov. 23, when the waxing gibbous moon will move close to the nearby Pleiades, its strong light reducing the number of faint stars visible around them. Use binoculars to find some of its hundreds of stars.

It has been revealed that I'm a stargazer and not at all interested in Greek mythology, but it sometimes helps to know a few basic ancient myths when finding constellations. A good example is the constellation Cepheus. It's named after a king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda — all three of which are close by in the northern sky right now. Look west after dark, away from the bright moon, to find the Summer Triangle — Vega, Deneb and Altair — which by now is sinking into the west. From Deneb, look north for a distinctive five-star pattern resembling a child's drawing of a house, with a square base and pointed roof. That's Cepheus. Its brightest star is Alderamin, about 49 light-years away, which marks one corner of the "house.".

He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

United Airlines on Monday remarked it had resolved a "widespread system outage" that briefly affected departing flights.

Sources indicate that "We have resolved a technology glitch that delayed flight departures," the airline stated in a statement. "While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights.

A United spokesperson remarked there was no indication that the outage was a cyberattack.

The Air Line Pilots Association, which represents pilots for United and other carriers, said in an earlier message to members seen by CNBC that the operational outage was "affecting multiple pilot facing applications" and that United could not "provide outbound flights with final weights.".

United's outage came three days after a nationwide ground stop halted departures across the country for more than four hours, snarling travel and leading to widespread delays and cancellations over the weekend.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the issues that led to Friday's ground stop on a router in Arkansas that overwhelmed systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control. Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford remarked the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over from copper wires to fiber optic.

There were significantly fewer flight delays and cancellations Monday than had been reported Sunday, according to FlightAware data.

There was no indication that United's outage Monday was related to the complications that caused Friday's ground stop.

— CNBC's Leslie Josephs and Phil LeBeau contributed to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free.

  • In a recent development, look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free. Back in July 2026, DW reported how one epidemiologist had suggested an 'amnesia' about the measles risk was pushing a growth in US infections.

According to recent reports, four months later, it was official. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) said the US had lost its measles elimination status, along with Mexico.

But it doesn't have to stay this way.

In a recent development, look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status. But within five years — during the COVID-19 pandemic — it fought and won back its measles-free status. And since 2024, Brazil has stayed measles-free, even as the highly contagious disease spread across the rest of the Americas.

In 2026, with the data available up to the time of writing this article, Brazil had only had 70 measles cases. They were all linked to infections brought in from abroad, often from neighboring Peru.

Sources indicate that brazil has fewer people than the US, about 213 million compared to the US's nearly 350 million, but the two countries are similar in size. So the comparison is worth considering.

Brazil moves fast. The PAHO asks countries to respond within 72 hours of a suspected measles case. Here's Brazil's own rule:.

It has also made hunting for cases a national habit. In a program called "Dia S," health workers knock on doors and visit schools, daycare centers and churches to find people who may be sick but have not seen a doctor.

Brazil also holds mass vaccination days called "Dia D." There was one in November, in the area where Brazil borders Colombia and Peru.

If someone is diagnosed with measles, health workers try to track down every person the patient may have met ("contact persons") and vaccinate them and other people living nearby.

The country has so far provided more than 16 million doses of the measles vaccine in 2026 and has donated 500,000 doses to Peru.

Brazil isn't perfect, though. According to official estimates from the World Health Organization, only 76% of children got both required doses of the vaccine in 2025 — well short of the 95% target. Experts warn this leaves the country at risk because measles is so highly contagious. A country needs to be as close to 100% immunized as possible to protect people and stop the disease from spreading.

"Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf. It must be protected every day," notes PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that the US lost its measles-free status because the PAHO found that the same strain of the virus had been spreading in the country for 12 months or more. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status on the same day as the US.

It has been revealed that the US has had more than 5,400 cases in 2026 (at time of writing), more than twice as many as in all of 2025, and about 19 times as many as in 2024. Nearly everyone who got sick with measles was unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status.

According to recent reports, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on new vaccination recommendations for children in August 2026. It came at a time, when, as we reported, experts noted people had stopped getting vaccinated against measles because infection rates were low. But like PAHO's Barbosa said, neglecting vaccination when infection rates are low is a mistake.

To be fair, Trump's executive order listed the measles vaccine in a top category of vaccinations recommended for every child. But the administration's stance on vaccination in general is unclear.

Industry observers note that health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has often declared opposition to vaccination, including against measles, advising people to take vitamin A instead. In Texas, this led to children being hospitalized with toxic levels of the supplement, and left them with no protection against measles.

Sources indicate that before the COVID-19 pandemic, 95% of US kindergartners had their measles shots. Now, it's 92%, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Protection (CDC). That leaves about 280,000 kindergartners in the US unprotected.

In the Texas counties where a 2025 measles outbreak began, coverage was as low as 77% at the time.

US children usually need vaccines to start school, but most states let parents opt out for religious or personal reasons, with no doctor involved.

In a recent development, but vaccination rates have fallen elsewhere in the world as well, including in Europe. In Germany, where measles infections have also risen, experts blame anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Industry observers note that A person sick with measles can infect up to18 other, unprotected people. With vaccination, it is possible to increase the number of protected people and lower the number of people the sick person can infect.

To prevent a measles outbreak, a community needs about 95% of people to be vaccinated and/or immune. The vaccination consists of two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine.

But even after the two doses, a person can expect to have only 97% protection against measles — 3% short of full protection — so, nearly everyone in the community has to be vaccinated to keep the average level of protect as close to 100% as possible.

"For some diseases like measles, even a small decrease in vaccination rates can lead to more outbreaks of disease [so] community immunity requires over 95% of susceptible individuals to be immunized," says Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

Sources indicate that and the 95% has to hold everywhere. A good national average can be affected by, for example, a single school where only 70% of the children are vaccinated. And that is where the outbreak is likely to start.

Around the world, measles deaths have dropped by 88% since 2000, thanks to vaccines.

But progress has stalled. Only about three out of four children worldwide get both doses of the vaccine. The biggest outbreaks right now are in Bangladesh, Indonesia and Guatemala.

Recent findings suggest that data from Europe highlights that things can get better. In the European Union, cases fell from more than 35,000 in 2024 to about 2,300 the following year, with no measles-related deaths.

Romania went from more than 30,000 cases in 2024 to about 4,200 in 2025.

In Hungary, where 99% of children are vaccinated, there have been no measles cases in the past year.

According to recent reports, but in January, six European countries lost their measles-free status, including the UK, Spain and Austria. Across Europe, eight out of ten people who got measles in 2025 were unvaccinated.

The Americas are seeing a major surge in measles infections, with more than 58,000 cases in 2026, over four times as many as by November in 2025. Guatemala has been hit hardest, with almost 35,000 cases.

The deadliest outbreaks are in Africa. African Union countries have so far reported nearly 1,800 measles deaths in 2026, about 1,650 of them in Democratic Republic of Congo. Yet, Sudan, despite the war, raised first-dose measles coverage by 22 percentage points in 2025, which was the world's largest gain.

Sources indicate that measles is extremely contagious. One person can infect up to 18 unprotected people, which makes it about 12 times more contagious than the flu.

The virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after a sick person has left the room. And people spread it before they know they are sick. Someone with measles is contagious for four days before the rash appears and four days after.

It has been revealed that it's not just a rash. About one in five unvaccinated people who get measles in the US ends up in the hospital. Measles can weaken the immune system for years, making it harder to fight off other infections.

But it's preventable. Two doses of the MMR vaccine (which also protects against mumps and rubella) protect 97% of people for life.

Industry News: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alzheimer's disease may begin leaving detectable clues in the brain as much as a decade before memory problems appear.
  • The discovery could eventually help doctors recognize Alzheimer's years before symptoms develop, potentially allowing treatment to begin when it has the greatest chance of protecting the brain.
  • By examining hundreds of brain scans, the scientists found that the entorhinal cortex and amygdala, two regions involved in memory and emotion, begin losing tissue earlier than the hippocampus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alzheimer's disease may begin leaving detectable clues in the brain as much as a decade before memory problems appear. Researchers at Johns Hopkins University have identified two brain regions that show signs of deterioration earlier than the hippocampus, the area commonly examined for evidence of the disease.

The discovery could eventually help doctors recognize Alzheimer's years before symptoms develop, potentially allowing treatment to begin when it has the greatest chance of protecting the brain.

By examining hundreds of brain scans, the scientists found that the entorhinal cortex and amygdala, two regions involved in memory and emotion, begin losing tissue earlier than the hippocampus. These changes may offer important fresh clues about how Alzheimer's develops and how it could be detected before significant cognitive decline occurs.

Industry observers note that "We have found that there are early changes in the brain manifesting the clinical biomarkers of atrophy as much as a decade before there are clinical symptoms," said biomedical engineer and senior author Michael Miller. "It's at least a 5-to-10-year play where your brain is changing. Imagine if we could start to treat the neurodegenerative changes at the 2, 3 or 4-year point rather than after 15 years when the changes are manifesting in memory symptoms. That's the great promise here for your loved ones who are at risk.".

The findings were recently published in NeuroImage Reports and are being presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience.

Detecting Alzheimer's Before Memory Loss Begins.

According to recent reports, alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia worldwide, but the disease does not begin when someone first experiences forgetfulness or confusion. Changes associated with Alzheimer's can accumulate in the brain for decades before noticeable symptoms emerge.

In a recent development, scientists believe this long period of silent progression may provide a crucial opportunity for treatment. Interventions that begin before extensive damage occurs could potentially do more to preserve memory and other cognitive abilities. However, taking advantage of that opportunity requires reliable ways to identify the disease in its earliest stages.

Recent findings suggest that one promising approach involves biomarkers, measurable biological changes that can indicate the presence or progression of a disease. In Alzheimer's research, these markers could help reveal who is developing the condition before symptoms become apparent.

"Our goal is to be able to treat individuals before the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease develop so that they may delayed or even stopped," noted Marilyn Albert, co-author and director of the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer's Disease Research Center.

Two Brain Regions Reveal Earlier Warning Signs.

To investigate where the earliest detectable changes occur, the researchers examined hundreds of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) scans collected through two independent research projects: the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative and the Biomarkers of Cognitive Decline Among Normal Individuals study.

The scans followed people at different stages of Alzheimer's disease over time, including individuals without symptoms, those experiencing cognitive impairment, and patients who ultimately died from the disease.

Sources indicate that in both groups, the researchers observed a consistent pattern. The entorhinal cortex and amygdala, which are located near the hippocampus, revealed greater relative tissue loss during the early stages of Alzheimer's than the hippocampus itself.

This distinction matters because the hippocampus plays a central role in memory and has traditionally been a major focus when doctors look for Alzheimer's-related brain damage.

Sources indicate that the two newly highlighted regions perform important functions of their own. The entorhinal cortex helps retrieve previously stored memories, while the amygdala contributes to emotional memory, including how emotional experiences are processed and remembered.

Their earlier shrinkage suggests that examining these structures together could reveal signs of Alzheimer's that might be less apparent when attention is focused primarily on the hippocampus.

Brain Shrinkage Linked to Alzheimer's Tau Protein.

The researchers also found an important connection between the loss of brain tissue and tau, a protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Under normal conditions, tau helps maintain the internal structure of nerve cells. In Alzheimer's, however, tau can accumulate abnormally and form tangles that interfere with healthy brain function.

Recent findings suggest that using PET imaging and digital pathology, the scientists found that areas of gray matter shrinkage overlapped with regions showing tau-related changes. Gray matter contains large numbers of nerve cell bodies and is essential for processing information throughout the brain.

This relationship strengthens the possibility that changes in the entorhinal cortex and amygdala could serve as useful indicators of early Alzheimer's disease.

The team believes that measuring tissue loss in both regions, rather than relying primarily on changes in the hippocampus, could eventually improve predictions of who is likely to develop cognitive decline.

It has been revealed that as brain imaging becomes more accessible and less expensive, this approach could also become increasingly practical. For people with a family history of Alzheimer's or other risk factors, researchers envision a future in which doctors might examine these regions as early as a person's 30s or 40s.

"As biomarkers and treatments become increasingly available, knowing who is going to have cognitive decline is going to be really key," mentioned co-author Meaghan Morris, a neuropathologist who studies Alzheimer's and other dementias. "This could really play into better risk stratification for identifying who is going to have cognitive decline in the near future -- and treating people earlier and earlier to hopefully slow the course of the disease.".

A Potential Latest Path Toward Earlier Alzheimer's Treatment.

Recent findings suggest that although the findings are promising, more research is necessary before doctors can use these brain changes as a reliable diagnostic tool. The study identifies potential early biomarkers, but it does not yet establish a clinical test capable of predicting Alzheimer's years in advance.

The next step is to investigate what happens within these regions at a much smaller scale. The researchers want to understand the molecular changes surrounding abnormal tau accumulation and how those changes contribute to the progressive loss of brain tissue.

Identifying the biological processes involved could eventually reveal new targets for therapies designed to interrupt Alzheimer's before extensive damage occurs.

"Our future work is to better show the molecular neighborhoods associated with these Tau protein changes as localized by these clinical biomarkers of atrophy," Miller stated. "Once we know more about the molecular neighborhoods, we can develop therapies.".

#59192. ‘I had felt overconfident’: senior scientists reveal mistakes that aided discovery

‘I had felt overconfident’: senior scientists reveal mistakes that aided discovery

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physicist Peter Shawhan and his team perfected not finding gravitational waves at the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) facility in Livingston, Louisiana — until they did.
  • Sources indicate that to err is human, science endeavours included.
  • Sometimes, reaching a dead end was the only way around a problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physicist Peter Shawhan and his team perfected not finding gravitational waves at the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) facility in Livingston, Louisiana — until they did. Credit: Igor Andreoni/Peter Shawhan.

Sources indicate that to err is human, science endeavours included. Accounts of missteps in the laboratory or field abound among early-career researchers, as do tales of what they learnt from them. But senior scientists make mistakes, too — and not just early in their careers.

Sometimes, reaching a dead end was the only way around a problem. Other times, graduate students saved their advisers from throwing away ‘wrong’ data. Senior scientists also know the dangers of overthinking and how it can lead to experimental paralysis. “Every year, I devote a meeting with students and postdocs to discuss failures and how errors of judgement or methods are part of academic life,” claims Catherine Badgley, a palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. “I hope this helps them to see they can learn from mistakes rather than be devastated by them.”.

Nature’s careers team spoke to Badgley and four other senior scientists to hear about their ‘failures’ and the lessons they took from them.

Physicist at the University of Maryland in College Park and a deputy spokesperson for the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) scientific collaboration.

For the past 26 years, I have been searching for gravitational waves with LIGO, which has a gravitational-wave observatory in Livingston, Louisiana. These waves are echoes of massive events such as the merging of black holes or the collision of neutron stars. They produce ripples in space-time and, by the time these tiny ripples reach Earth, they are so faint that scientists need extra help to ‘hear’ them, because they are extremely hard to detect by just using light, or telescopes, to see them. For example, observations of a collision of two neutron stars with telescopes has revealed the presence of gold and platinum atoms, solving a long-standing question: what is the origin of about half of all elements heavier than iron? The detection of such an event with LIGO would get us even more information.

In the first tests of LIGO, the team found nothing. Later, with improved detectors, we still found nothing.

In fact, we got very good at reporting nothing. We became experienced with knowing what we could rule out. By the time we made our first wave detection, in 2015, a finding that earned LIGO founders a physics Nobel in 2017, we had published about 100 papers reporting null results.

In a recent development, one such null case was in 2010. We were completing a science run, in which data are collected for a set period of time, and had a candidate for a striking event — it looked like we’d finally got there. But we knew it might be a ‘blind injection’, which is when a false signal is inserted into a data set by authorized colleagues to test our analyses.

In a recent development, we finished the analysis, drafted the paper and then asked the LIGO director to open a sealed envelope to tell us whether this was a real event or not. It wasn’t, but the exercise highlighted a real problem: the sky location our analysis recovered didn’t match the signal’s known location. Two of the detector’s mirrors had moved in the wrong direction. We found the glitch in about a day. This showed we could efficiently self-correct when detecting a real sign — which happened five years later.

I tell my students that scientists make lots of mistakes. We’re careful with cross-checks and analyse results carefully, so we catch almost all of them. Some are caught in minutes, some in days and some take more work. This one, because we’d built a test designed to assess itself, took about a day. That’s really the goal: not avoiding mistakes, but rather building enough ways to catch them quickly. Knowing what it means to find nothing is important; it’s a real scientific skill.

Chemist Omar Yaghi (second row, fifth from right), with his team at Tsinghua University in Beijing, says that professors can learn key lessons from their students if they listen to them.Credit: Yaghi Group Photo.

Chemist at Tsinghua University in Beijing and a co-recipient of the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work with metal–organic frameworks.

In a recent development, back in the 1990s, I was an assistant professor at Arizona State University in Tempe. My team had begun research trying to make inorganic porous materials. These are solid materials with a network of tiny, connected pores that act like molecular sponges to trap molecules, such as wastewater contaminants and toxic gases, on their surfaces. We were successful: we had a paper1 published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society and, later, in Science2.

According to recent reports, then a doctoral student came looking to join my lab. She didn’t sound very confident, her English was not so good and it wasn’t the right time of year to look for a PhD adviser. I made up some reason not to take her. But she kept coming back and was adamant about working with me.

Recent findings suggest that so I accepted her into my lab group, and she started working on metal–organic compounds, another type of porous material. I felt that this was a waste of time: researchers had known about these structures since the 1950s, but nothing useful had resulted from them. Once you emptied their solvent-filled pores to trap other molecules, such as gases, they collapsed and became useless. I used to call them sculptures: they had beauty, but no function.

Sources indicate that she kept at it, and I held onto my scepticism. After a year, we sat down to discuss her results. That was when I realized that there was an opportunity there: we could make robust metal–organic compounds, after all.

Sources indicate that metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are also materials full of tiny pores. But what makes them particularly interesting is that scientists can adjust the size and shape of those pores, as well as the chemical properties inside them. This makes MOFs more tunable than inorganic porous materials such as zeolites and much better at trapping some gases. Some MOFs can drive chemical reactions, some conduct electricity and some are stable enough to be reused.

My student found strong chemical bindings that gave stability to early versions of these structures and, within a very short period, our findings were published in Nature3. It had worked.

Decades later, I met with my former student, and she told me that she had been struggling back then and wanted to try her luck with me, a upcoming professor at the time, because no one else would take her in.

I think science is the greatest equalizer. One discovery can take you from humble beginnings, as it did for us, and propel you to the top of your profession.

I had an opinion about an area of research and didn’t listen to my student, and, to that student’s credit, she persisted. To my credit, I changed my thinking. Neither the student nor the professor can afford to do science without the other.

Recent findings suggest that plant geneticist Chris Martine’s misidentified sample led to the identification of a newly introduced species of bush tomato plant in northern Australia. Credit: Jason Cantley.

Plant geneticist at Bucknell University in Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, and president of the Botanical Society of America.

Industry observers note that I’ve studied Australia’s bush tomatoes for about 25 years. My team was the first to describe Solanum ossicruentum, nicknamed the blood bone tomato because it seems to bleed when cut open. It got us some press coverage and was a massive deal for our laboratory in 20164.

In 2017, Angela McDonnell, a postdoc, joined us. We started a substantial genetics project to build an evolutionary tree to understand the family history of the bush tomatoes we had been studying for years. We had two samples of S. ossicruentum from two locations: the Tanami Desert and the Keep River National Park, both in northern Australia. When the results of testing came back, genomic differences landed them in totally different places on the evolutionary tree of the group.

According to recent reports, in my mind, there was no way it was possible. I’d identified the specimens myself. I assumed we’d mislabelled something. I asked Angela to check everything carefully, but she was certain that wasn’t the case. To me it didn’t add up — I came close to saying, “let’s just pull the misplaced one and call it an error”.

According to recent reports, two years ago, while looking through the folders of S. ossicruentum specimens at the Northern Territory Herbarium in Palmerston, Australia, I noticed some that had strange dots on the backs of their leaves. At first, I thought it was mildew, but then I wondered whether these dots were extrafloral nectaries, or nectar-producing glands found outside the plant’s flower. Then I realized the plants with such dots were mostly from one part of Australia, the northern edge of the Tanami Desert — exactly where I was heading next.

Industry observers note that when I got there, plants with these little dots were dripping with nectar with ants harvesting it, an interaction I hadn’t seen to this level before. I checked whether Angela’s major phylogeny project had anything from that region, and there it was — the misplaced plant. The two samples of what I thought were S. ossicruentum belonged in two different places on the evolutionary tree because they were two different species. Indeed, that initial sample’s evolutionary tree placement was the best evidence for the new species that we later described: Solanum nectarifolium5. My first thought was to thank Angela for not pulling that specimen out of our analysis. I was honestly thrilled.

In a recent development, before that, I had felt overconfident in what I knew, and Angela was certain that this was a carefully curated data set and a rigorously achieved genetic result. As I’ve become more senior, I’ve become more comfortable with uncertainty: when something doesn’t fit our preconceived ideas, that’s an interesting result — that’s how you find more upcoming things.

It has been revealed that now I realize how notable it is for people who are more junior than myself to speak up and share their ideas, especially when they run counter to convention. If we look back at the history of science, that’s the only way we’ve progressed.

Palaeontologist Catherine Badgley claims that a key skill for scientists is knowing when to stop pursuing a good idea that simply isn’t working. Credit: David Bay.

Palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor.

It has been revealed that in the 1990s, I was an associate research scientist in the University of Michigan’s Museum of Paleontology. Serge Legendre, a colleague who was then at the University of Montpellier in France, revealed me a fresh way, at the time, of explaining body-size distributions in fossils of extinct mammalian species. He used cenograms — a graphical technique that ranks mammalian species in a community by body size.

Sources indicate that in well-watered ecosystems, there was a fairly continuous line: all species were closely spaced in size. But habitats with long dry seasons had a major gap in the middle where medium-sized mammals would be — an interesting mystery. Legendre found that many animals in that size range are fruit-eaters, and fruit isn’t available in arid or very cold environments all year long. If the theory was correct, we might be able to infer past climate from the sizes of mammals in fossil communities.

I had a lot of climate data for mammal locations worldwide, so the two of us, as well as palaeontologist Philip Gingerich, who was then also at the University of Michigan, decided to build a much larger database of locations and add climate variables. We wanted to determine whether climate variables could predict the size gap we saw. I was excited enough that I wrote it up as a book proposal and received a contract from the University of Chicago Press.

According to recent reports, but the more data that we collected, the fuzzier the picture became. After more than a year, I had written four chapters. But I had to admit we had fewer results than when we started.

I knew the data weren’t flawed because I had used this enormous mammalian fossil database successfully for other research projects. For example, undergraduate students used it to show that the length of the growing season, as a climate variable, could be used to predict the number of fruit- and plant-eating species at a given time.

It has been revealed that I eventually realized that each continent has its own evolutionary history and its own climatic circumstances — no one is exactly like another. Our largest data sets, from Africa and North America, have almost completely non-overlapping climates, so one was never going to be a good model for predicting the other.

Tech Report: The Boox Picco made me love tiny e-readers

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I don't get the hype of tiny e-readers.
  • It has been revealed that boox is one of the first major brands to launch a mini e-reader of its own, the Picco.
  • The physical design of the Boox Picco isn't all that different from other tiny e-readers, but what matters is literally what's on the inside.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I don't get the hype of tiny e-readers. I've used a ton of e-readers — Kindles, Kobos, and Boox — and I thought they were just the right size, and I wasn't craving a smaller e-reader. But plenty of people clearly are, as I've spent hours browsing Reddit and reading about how people use their tiny e-readers.

It has been revealed that boox is one of the first major brands to launch a mini e-reader of its own, the Picco. Other Boox e-readers run on Android, but the Picco does not. I expected to be underwhelmed, but I'm glad to be wrong. The Boox Picco has given me a whole upcoming love for tiny e-readers, and I finally understand their appeal.

The physical design of the Boox Picco isn't all that different from other tiny e-readers, but what matters is literally what's on the inside. The user interface is exceptionally easy to navigate and straightforward — it's pretty pared back compared to Kindle or Kobo.

In a recent development, the Picco combines physical buttons and touchscreen controls. The 'bookshelf' section is the device's native library. 'Transfer' lets you move books from the Boox Tile app on your phone to the device; 'Apps' offers a limited selection of pre-downloaded apps; and 'Settings' is exactly as it indicates. You can even set any photo as your lock screen, but keep in mind that the Boox Picco display is black-and-white only.

You can easily move to the home screen by swiping up, and swipe down to adjust brightness and warmth. Plus, it has two side buttons, which serve as page-turn buttons. The Pico is super responsive and loads pages quickly. I was worried I'd get overwhelmed by all the controls, but it's so intuitive that I quickly took to it and was navigating like it was second nature.

There isn't much to navigate on the device, but that's part of what makes it so easy. It's all about keeping you focused with apps like a to-do list and a Pomodoro timer.

Sources indicate that if you've used other e-readers, you might be used to devices from the same brand speaking to each other. So Boox e-reader users might expect the Picco to sync with other Boox models. Unfortunately, that's not the case. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Boox Picco only connects to WiFi temporarily to transfer files. Since it doesn't maintain a connection, it won't frequently patch to reflect whatever's in your Boox library. This also means that it won't update your progress in a book across e-readers, so you'll have to manually turn the page to catch up when you switch devices.

With a 3.97-inch screen, it's an incredibly small e-reader designed to literally fit on the back of your phone. While other tiny e-readers have promised the same, the Boox Picco really does. Its MagSafe case is perfectly positioned so it attaches conveniently without hanging off the side. Keep in mind, though, it fits best on an iPhone Pro Max (pictured below).

Sources indicate that it feels very sturdy, too, living up to its $110 price tag. Weighing two ounces, it has a slight heft so it doesn't feel like it'll slip out of your hand, but it also doesn't add too much weight to your phone when attached.

Tiny e-readers have one massive overarching issue, so this isn't exclusive to the Boox Picco, but you're only able to read DRM-free EPUB files. Typically, these e-books are only in the public domain, so you're extremely limited in what you can read on the device. That means any EPUBs you borrowed on Libby or purchased on Kindle or Kobo can't be uploaded to the Boox Picco.

So, for most e-reader consumers, the Boox Picco won't align with their reading habits.

Yes, the Boox Picco is the tiny e-reader worth buying — although it won't be for everyone. You need to temper your expectations about what you can read on it, as it only supports DRM-free EPUBs. But if you're reading DRM-free EPUBs on your e-reader anyway, then the Boox Picco is a fun device to add to your repertoire.

It has been revealed that it's well-designed inside and out, with a sturdy case that snaps onto MagSafe devices, and an easy-to-navigate user interface. At $109.99, it's cheaper than most e-readers we've tested, which feels on par for a device that is smaller and possesses fewer capabilities than a standard e-reader. And if you're deciding between an Xteink e-reader and the Boox Picco — go for the Picco. It's far more user-friendly.

#59188. Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form.
  • Although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean.
  • Polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. These rocks, known as polymetallic nodules, contain miniature cracks and cavities that provide shelter for creatures smaller than a millimeter.

Although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean. They create hard surfaces in an environment dominated by soft mud, while their internal spaces provide additional habitats for marine life.

Polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides. They grow at an extraordinarily slow pace, often adding only a few millimeters over a million years. Found at ocean depths ranging from 4,000 to 6,000 meters, they can remain on the seafloor for millions of years.

Researchers set out to investigate the tiny organisms living within these ancient formations and determine how vital the nodules are to deep-sea biodiversity.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Tanja Stratmann, a deep-sea ecologist and one of the study's three lead authors, explains: "In our study we show that the sizes of cracks inside the nodules are large enough to provide home to animals that are smaller than a millimeter in size.".

Hundreds of Tiny Animals Found Inside a Single Rock.

To explore these hidden habitats, the research team collected nodules from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a vast region of the central Pacific Ocean. They used specialized sampling equipment, including box corers that collect sections of the seafloor and remotely operated diving robots capable of working at extreme depths.

Back in the laboratory, the researchers carefully opened the nodules and extracted the tiny animals concealed within their cracks and crevices.

Recent findings suggest that the results revealed an unexpectedly rich community of marine life. Across 244 nodules, the team identified 4,139 individual animals. Each nodule contained an average of 17 animals, but one particularly crowded specimen sheltered an astonishing 245 individuals.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery reveals that these rocks are more than simple surfaces where marine organisms can attach themselves. Their intricate internal structures create three-dimensional living spaces, allowing animals to inhabit protected areas within the nodules themselves.

In a recent development, dr. Coral Diaz-Recio Lorenzo explains: "The crevices in the polymetallic nodules function as small shelters and provide home to animals that we do not encounter in the soft sediment of the seafloor.".

Hidden Ecosystems Unlike Those on the Surrounding Seafloor.

Although the nodules contained fewer animals than the surrounding muddy sediment, their contribution to deep-sea life was still substantial.

For roundworms (nematodes), the number living inside the nodules amounted to approximately 10% of the number found in the surrounding sediment. For tiny crustaceans (copepods), the figure was about 25%.

However, the most important finding was not simply how many animals the researchers discovered. It was how different the communities inside the rocks were from those living in the nearby mud.

Industry observers note that genetic analyses revealed that the animals inhabiting the nodules formed distinctive communities. Remarkably, these communities remained highly similar across locations separated by large distances (up to 1,000 km), even though they differed significantly from the organisms found in the surrounding seafloor sediment.

This suggests that polymetallic nodules support specialized habitats that are not easily replaced by other parts of the deep ocean. Their cracks and cavities offer living conditions that certain organisms appear to depend on.

Deep-Sea Mining Could Destroy These Ancient Habitats.

The findings raise serious concerns about the potential environmental consequences of deep-sea mining.

According to recent reports, polymetallic nodules contain economically valuable metals, including nickel, cobalt, and copper. These resources have attracted interest in industrial mining operations that would collect the nodules directly from the ocean floor.

However, removing the rocks would also eliminate the miniature habitats they contain, along with the animals living inside them.

One example is Thurammina sp. 1, a single-celled organism found particularly frequently within the nodules. This species appears especially well adapted to the sheltered spaces inside the rocks, making it an example of the specialized life that could be threatened by their removal.

Industry observers note that the problem is that these habitats cannot quickly recover. Because polymetallic nodules require millions of years to develop, new ones would not form within a human lifetime. Mining could therefore eliminate ecosystems that would take geological timescales to replace.

Industry observers note that prof. Sabine Gollner warns: "Our findings point out that commercial mining may result in an irreversible loss of undescribed and unique biodiversity associated to nodules. This needs to be considered in environmental management of deep-sea mining.".

Scientists Race to Understand What Could Be Lost.

In a recent development, the discovery highlights an often overlooked aspect of ocean conservation. Protecting deep-sea ecosystems requires more than safeguarding large, visible animals. It also means considering the microscopic and nearly microscopic organisms that inhabit specialized environments hidden within the seafloor.

An important question remains unanswered: If deep-sea mining destroys these nodule communities, could some species disappear entirely?

In a recent development, researchers still need to determine whether organisms that depend on the nodules also inhabit other parts of the ocean. If certain species are restricted to these habitats, removing the nodules could potentially contribute to their global extinction.

Understanding where these animals live and how widely they are distributed will be essential for identifying areas that need protection and evaluating the potential ecological damage caused by deep-sea mining.

Industry observers note that to investigate further, Dr. Tanja Stratmann is right now participating in an international research expedition to the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, where scientists are continuing to study the ecosystems associated with polymetallic nodules.

This expedition and other follow-up investigations are independently funded through the JPIOcean projects MiningImpact 2 and 3.

Sources indicate that the findings reveal that even a single rock on the deep ocean floor can support a surprisingly complex community of life. As interest in harvesting the ocean's mineral resources grows, scientists are working to understand these hidden ecosystems before habitats that took millions of years to form are permanently lost.
