10 things that worry me about chasing the 2027 total solar eclipse in Egypt

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1627 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 2, 2027, I'll be in Luxor, Egypt, to witness what could be the greatest total solar eclipse of my life.
  • According to recent reports, I've been calling it the "eclipse of the century" for many years, and for good reason.
  • According to recent reports, I've chased eclipses long enough to know that the celestial mechanics are the easy part.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on Aug. 2, 2027, I'll be in Luxor, Egypt, to witness what could be the greatest total solar eclipse of my life. I've seen nine total solar eclipses across the world, but this one promises to be different. For a remarkable six minutes and 22 seconds, the moon will completely cover the sun, plunging Egypt's ancient temples and monuments into eerie twilight as the solar corona bursts into view.

According to recent reports, I've been calling it the "eclipse of the century" for many years, and for good reason. It will be the longest total solar eclipse until 2114 — and the longest on land of the 21st century — and it will take place in one of the most extraordinary places on Earth. What could go wrong?

According to recent reports, I've chased eclipses long enough to know that the celestial mechanics are the easy part. The moon will arrive exactly on schedule — that's guaranteed. Everything else — the weather, the crowds, the transport, the equipment and the people — is rather less predictable. From the possibility of dust storms to uncertainty about whether boats will even be allowed to move on the Nile, there are plenty of reasons to be slightly wary about what awaits eclipse chasers after the ultimate bragging rights on Aug. 2, 2027. Here are the 10 things worrying me most about the 2027 total solar eclipse in Egypt.

The chances of cloud-free skies in Luxor and anywhere in Upper Egypt in August are exceptionally high — close to 100%. That's almost unheard of in eclipse-chasing. However, clouds aren't the only thing that can obscure the sun. Dust and sand are potential hazards in the Egyptian desert, and a dust storm at the wrong moment could affect—though probably not ruin—the view. Although the sun will almost certainly be visible during the eclipse, airborne dust could hide the delicate structure of the solar corona.

Industry observers note that how many people will descend on Luxor for the eclipse? August is normally a quiet month for tourism in Luxor because of the oppressive heat. In 2027, however, the city and its surrounding urban area — population about four million — could swell as eclipse chasers, tour groups, photographers and curious visitors descend. Hotels, roads, buses and archaeological sites will all face extraordinary pressure. My biggest concern isn't necessarily the number of people watching the eclipse, but the logistical chaos it will create. Let's take Mallorca as an example for the 2026 eclipse. Authorities there had a plan for its west coast, the prime viewing region. "They were going to start closing roads from 3 p.m. on the afternoon of the eclipse," noted Simon Waldram, who runs astrophotography and landscape photography workshops and who drove his tour group to the intended viewing location at 8 o'clock on the morning of the eclipse. "There were already 300 cars there, and by 11 a.m. they had shut the road." Official aims can rapidly change.

It has been revealed that luxor in August is brutally hot. Temperatures can exceed 104 degrees Fahrenheit (40 degrees Celsius). Totality will strike at 1:02 p.m. local time (EEST). During the eclipse, from 11:40 a.m. to 2:26 p.m., the sun will be almost directly overhead. Many tour groups will stay on their hotel grounds or remain on cruise ships — relatively close to shade and air-con — though I'm also planning to keep a wet towel around my neck and carry plenty of water. However, the heat will affect the entire trip. "We're planning our visits in the early mornings and in the late afternoon, with midday just quiet time," stated Khaled ElSamman, an Egyptologist at Nord Nile whose tour will witness the eclipse from a traditional dahabiya, a two-masted river boat, in Luxor. "There are reminders to drink water and keep hydrated, but it's easy to forget if you're not used to the environment and this much humidity loss.".

Recent findings suggest that I'll be traveling on the Nile, which sounds like a wonderfully romantic way to experience an eclipse. However, there's speculation that river traffic could be restricted, perhaps even from the previous day. "There might be a restriction on navigation on the Nile during the eclipse, so it's a bit hard to strategy where we are going to watch it," stated ElSamman. "We might end up in harbor, and maybe we won't be allowed to be in the middle of the water.".

Even if we're safely moored in Luxor, how many other vessels will be there? The Nile looks set to be packed with cruise ships, traditional dahabiyas and smaller boats, all carrying people hoping to witness the same extraordinary event. I wonder what totality will actually look and sound like. Will there be music? Shouting? Bright lights from neighboring boats? Probably — though perhaps that's no bad thing. It's fun to experience totality in all kinds of different environments. One of my most vivid memories of the 1999 total solar eclipse in the U.K. is the atmosphere created by the people around me and the lights that came on in boats in Falmouth harbor. Perhaps the noise and excitement will become part of the magic. I just hope nobody leaves their floodlights on.

It has been revealed that whether eclipse chasers can bring specialist camera equipment into the country is vexing many. After all, "professional-looking" camera equipment is usually difficult to get through customs. While phones and compact cameras are fine, customs and security personnel classify large mirrorless/DSLR cameras, long telephoto lenses and heavy tripods as "professional filming gear." My reporting suggests customs officials may take a more relaxed approach to specialist camera equipment during the eclipse. However, no special customs arrangements for eclipse visitors have been confirmed. Drones are a different matter — Egypt has strict restrictions on importing and operating them, with authorization required. Bringing a drone to see this eclipse would be a mistake.

Recent findings suggest that photographing a total solar eclipse involves pointing equipment towards the sun for an extended period, using appropriate solar filters during the partial phases. In Luxor's extreme August temperatures — and with the sun almost directly overhead — overheating could become a serious concern, particularly for cameras recording video or running continuously. Eclipse chasers will need to keep equipment shaded and as cool as possible. I'll just hope to have my trusty image-stabilized binoculars with me. I bought them a decade ago specifically for total solar eclipses, and they've given me some of the most extraordinary views and moments of my life.

It has been revealed that watching a total solar eclipse from Karnak or another ancient Egyptian temple sounds almost impossibly romantic. But the reality could be very different. Popular archaeological sites, such as Karnak, Luxor Temple, Hatshepsut and the Valley of the Kings, could be overwhelmed by visitors. That could mean crowded entrances, long queues and limited facilities. Besides, with the eclipsed sun close to the zenith, those spectacular images of totality framed between ancient columns may be more fantasy than reality. It may be wise to avoid the crowds — and with myriad temples and ruins near Luxor, that's likely possible. "You want to make sure you're not fighting with 10,000 other tourists trying to see the same thing," remarked Waldram. Queueing for hours at Karnak is not the best way to enjoy one of nature's greatest events.

Every eclipse chaser who aims and books a hotel years in advance dreads the email that often arrives a few weeks before, saying a reservation has been canceled for some spurious reason. Welcome to eclipse-gouging, when hotel, lodge and Airbnb owners realize the eclipse date and hike their prices. This has already happened in Luxor, where prices have already reached about $600 per person per night for the week of the eclipse — roughly seven times higher than usual. Worse, people expect prices to keep rising as the eclipse gets closer. Owners of remaining hotels and boats are now refusing to charter or commit, waiting for higher prices. In a country where the average wage is $150-200 per month, it's understandable — a total solar eclipse is potentially a unique jackpot for many. But it makes life a little harder for eclipse chasers.

Sources indicate that I've witnessed totality on a tennis court at sunset, standing next to a horse on a mountain and on a cruise ship in the Southern Ocean — among others — but I've never encountered the eclipsed sun almost directly overhead. I'll need to crane my neck to see it, and for a very long time. Should I lie flat on the ground? Recline on a boat deck? Or perhaps float in a swimming pool? I'm only half joking. Six minutes is a long time to stare almost vertically upward. Finding a comfortable position could make a surprisingly big difference to how much I enjoy the spectacle.

Sources indicate that to spend six uninterrupted minutes studying the sun's ghostly corona, watching its delicate streamers stretch into space, is almost beyond comprehension. And that's why, despite all my worries, the "eclipse of the century" can't come soon enough. "It will have hiccups," said ElSamman. "But it's going to be amazing.".

According to recent reports, jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#59060. Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1155 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • – Daisy, age 7, Upcoming York, New York.
  • A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day.
  • Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why do farts smell so bad? – Daisy, age 7, Upcoming York, New York.

A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day. Altogether, that’s enough gas to fill a super stinky party balloon.

Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut. These organisms have an key job: They help chew up food that your stomach cannot break down on its own. In the process, they act like mini chemical factories that provide you with nutrients while releasing waste gases into your gut. These gases mix with air you swallow and other gases that you make during digestion. After passing through the intestines, they come out in bursts as farts.

In a recent development, as a microbiologist, I study communities of bacteria, called microbiomes, in various regions of the human body. The microbiome in your gut plays an important role in your health. Producing gases is a sign that bacteria in the gut microbiome are doing their job properly. Farting also relieves pressure in your belly and prevents painful bloating and cramping.

So you might wonder: Why does a normal and healthy body process cause such a bad stink?

Farts are mostly made up of the same odorless gases found in the air we breathe.

It has been revealed that anywhere from 20% to 90% of a fart’s volume consists of nitrogen, which makes up more than three-quarters of air. Up to 10% of a fart is oxygen, which humans need in order to breathe. Up to 30% is carbon dioxide, up to 50% is hydrogen, and up to 10% is methane. Microbes produce most of the carbon dioxide, hydrogen and methane, though some of the carbon dioxide is made when digestive juices mix with stomach acid.

Recent findings suggest that but wait: These are not the gases that give farts their delightful array of aromas. What makes farts so malodorous is other gas molecules that contain the element sulfur. Pure sulfur has no smell on its own, but when combined with other elements it makes molecules that reek.

According to recent reports, one key culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which is famous for smelling like rotten eggs. Others include methanethiol, which has a bouquet of cabbage, sewage or skunk spray, and dimethyl sulfide, which hits the nostrils with scents of cooked corn, algae or seafood.

Industry observers note that only tiny amounts are required: One molecule of hydrogen sulfide among 1 million other gas molecules has enough power to do the job. That’s equivalent to one kernel of corn in a truckload of about 1,250 ears, or 10 bricks out of all the bricks that make up the Empire State Building in New York City. Other sulfur-containing gasses can be sniffed out at even more minuscule amounts.

The main thing that determines which gases and how much of them are in your farts is what food your gut microbiome gets to eat.

Some types of foods often referred to as junk food, including candy or diet foods containing artificial sweeteners or syrups, can change the way microbes digest food. High-fiber foods such as beans and grains also have this effect. These foods can cause your body to produce more farts that often are bigger and louder.

Sources indicate that however, the loudest fart is not always the stinkiest one. It’s the ones that contain sulfur that pack a smelly punch.

Food is a key source of amino acids, nutrients that build proteins the body needs to function and grow. Two amino acids, methionine and cysteine, contain sulfur, and they are plentiful in meat, dairy, eggs, and to a lesser degree, beans and grains. Some foods – most notably, vegetables such as cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower – contain other molecules that also have sulfur in them.

Industry observers note that when you eat sulfur-rich foods, your gut microbes digest them to produce sulfur-containing gases. That can lead to some putrid farts, with the precise smell tuned to your diet – as well as your overall health. In fact, persistent foul-smelling gas can be a sign of illness, such as irritable bowel syndrome or food intolerance or sensitivity, which you might need to see a doctor about.

According to recent reports, as you might know from experience, it’s impossible to hold in a fart until it goes away. It will come out somehow – sometimes at speeds up to 10 feet per second, according to back-of-the-envelope estimates, including my own. This rush of gas exiting the body makes the surrounding tissue vibrate, often causing an embarrassing noise.

Farting has been the butt of jokes for millennia. According to the Guinness Book of World Records, the oldest joke ever written down was a popular proverb dating back about 3,900 years that warned new husbands about their wives’ farts. The popularity of fart jokes remains strong. In the 2010 movie “Despicable Me,” for example, mad tech wizard Dr. Nefario mishears his boss’s demand for a dart gun, instead creating a fart gun, or Fart Blaster, that’s now a real-life popular toy.

But sometimes this natural body process can be a real bummer – like on an airplane. Cabin pressure in flight is often lower than normal air pressure on the ground, which can cause the gas in your gut to expand, spurring more farts. To protect the noses of travelers trapped together in the friendly skies, researchers designed seat cushions and blankets that contain sulfur-absorbing substances, such as activated charcoal. So far, no airlines have adopted these funk-reducing technologies, but you can buy them yourself.

Despite farts’ assault on the senses, your ability to detect them means your nose is doing exactly what evolution designed it to do: act as a chemical sensor for sulfur-containing gases. People can detect hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol at minuscule concentrations, even when there is less than one molecule of these compounds amid billions of other molecules.

These smells can signal the presence of rotting substances and bacterial activity that might harbor pathogens that can make you sick, or deadly environments such as swamps, stagnant caves and volcano vents that can suffocate and kill you.

So the next time you lay a fart that’s pungent enough to clear the room, don’t apologize – just say you’re conducting a live demonstration of natural chemistry that took eons of evolution to perfect.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.

The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data indicated with all ballots counted.

“We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo said in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.

He will get the first chance at forming a coalition to obtain majority in parliament as Marin’s era as prime minister was expected to end.

Popular abroad, at home Marin faces battle to keep her job.

It has been revealed that “We have gained support, we have gained more seats (in parliament). That’s an excellent achievement, even if we did not finish first today,” the prime minister stated in a speech to party members.

Marin, 37, the world’s youngest prime minister when she took office in 2019, is considered by fans around the globe as a millennial role model for progressive new leaders, but at home she has faced criticism for her partying and her government’s public spending.

Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin takes drug test following partying backlash.

While she remains very popular among many Finns, particularly young moderates, she antagonized some conservatives with lavish spending on pensions and education they see as not frugal enough.

It has been revealed that the NCP has led in polls for almost two years although its lead had melted away in recent months. It has promised to curb spending and stop the rise of public debt, which has reached just over 70% of GDP since Marin took office in 2019.

Orpo accused Marin of eroding Finland’s economic resilience at a time when Europe’s energy crisis, driven by Russia’s war in Ukraine, has hit the country hard and the cost of living has increased.

Orpo has stated he will negotiate with all groups to obtain a majority in parliament, while Marin has said her Social Democrats may govern with the NCP but will not go into government with the Finns Party.

Marin called the Finns Party “openly racist” during a debate in January – an accusation the nationalist group rejected.

The Finns Party’s main goal is to reduce what leader Riikka Purra has called “harmful” immigration from developing countries outside the European Union. It also calls for austerity policies to curb deficit spending, a stance it shares with the NCP.

Most notable of Marin’s foreign policy actions has been her push, along with President Sauli Niinisto, for the country to make a watershed policy U-turn by seeking NATO membership in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

That process is now almost complete, with Helsinki expected to join within days after all the Western defense alliance’s 30 members approved the accession.

#59055. Breaking: Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (879 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that imagine you’re in line at your favorite bakery, deciding whether to have a doughnut or a tart.
  • By the time you’re at the front of the line, however, only tarts are left.
  • These two decisions feel completely different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that imagine you’re in line at your favorite bakery, deciding whether to have a doughnut or a tart. You weigh them up, the doughnut wins, and you settle on that.

By the time you’re at the front of the line, however, only tarts are left. So, you buy one.

These two decisions feel completely different. One involves deliberation based on our unique and personal preferences, while the other involves simply recognizing and picking the only available option.

But our latest research published in the journal Imaging Neuroscience shows our brains actually make these decisions in surprisingly similar ways.

When we make free decisions, we recognize multiple options exist, weigh them up, and commit to one based on something internal: our preferences, values and goals.

According to recent reports, forced decisions are different. There’s only one possible outcome, and our job is simply to identify the option and take it.

Because free decisions feel so closely tied to who we are, neuroscientists have long assumed they rely on different processes in the brain compared to forced decisions. Some brain imaging studies support this, showing different patterns of neural activity distributed across the brain.

However, knowing where in the brain free choices happen tells us little about how they are formed – and whether this process is any different from forced decisions.

Decades of research have shown that, to make decisions, our brains gradually gather evidence for each option over time.

According to recent reports, think of it like a judge evaluating the facts of a case. Once enough evidence has been accumulated in favour of one party, a verdict is reached. For some types of decisions, this happens very quickly (over hundreds of milliseconds), making it feel like the choice just popped into your head.

By measuring electrical brain activity, researchers have identified a brain signal that reflects this accumulation of evidence during simple decisions – such as judging whether a traffic light is red or green.

Recent findings suggest that like a loading bar building to 100%, the signal gradually rises to a particular level before a decision is made. Because the action of neurons in the brain is noisy, this decision-making process also occurs in a noisy fashion: rather than climbing steadily towards one option, the signal fluctuates back and forth between the alternatives.

This partly explains why we aren’t always consistent with our choices – even when our preferences are stable, some days we will go for the tart and others, the doughnut.

This signal has been identified for forced decisions with a clear correct answer. But what about choices that are open-ended – shaped not just by what’s in front of us, but by something internal like preferences or personal goals?

In a recent development, to answer this question, we recorded people’s brain activity while they chose between sets of colored balloons. They viewed either two balloons of different colors to freely choose between, or a single balloon they were forced to pick.

They pressed a button the moment they made their choice, and we tracked how brain activity unfolded in the lead-up to that moment.

It has been revealed that for both free and forced decisions, the brain activity unfolded in a very similar way. Like a loading bar, it climbed steadily to the same peak level just before a choice was made. When people decided promptly, the signal increased faster. When they took longer, it rose more slowly.

That’s exactly what you would expect if the brain were tracking and weighing up evidence over time, rather than simply reacting to a decision at the last moment.

From this finding, one might assume the brain forms free and forced decisions in the same way, suggesting decision-making in the brain may be more automatic than it feels.

This echoes famous experiments by neuroscientist Benjamin Libet in the 1980s. He and colleagues found brain activity begins ramping up before people are even consciously aware of their intention to act – suggesting the brain has already begun deciding before the person consciously realizes they’ve made a choice.

But while the process may be automatic, what the brain is accumulating tells a different story. The evidence it weighs up is drawn entirely from who you are – your preferences, your goals, your experiences. Two people may go through the same neural process and land on the same choice, and yet arrive there for completely different reasons.

According to recent reports, so rather than asking whether our choices are truly free, perhaps the better question is what it really means for a choice to be yours. And the next time you find yourself in line at the bakery, know that your brain has already been quietly gathering evidence toward your baked good of choice, and that choice happens a little faster than you realize.

Moscow, meanwhile, confirmed a further strike on Friday night in Kryvyi Rih.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • False-colour view of Mercury produced using data from MESSENGER.Credit: NASA Goddard.
  • After an epic eight-year journey, the European and Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has arrived at Mercury.
  • Recent findings suggest that on 21 November, the European Space Agency (ESA) revealed that a European-built module had inserted itself into Mercury’s orbit, beginning a months-long series of manoeuvres.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

False-colour view of Mercury produced using data from MESSENGER.Credit: NASA Goddard.

After an epic eight-year journey, the European and Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has arrived at Mercury. It is only the second mission — after NASA’s MESSENGER in 2011–2015 — to enter orbit around the innermost planet of the Solar System.

Recent findings suggest that on 21 November, the European Space Agency (ESA) revealed that a European-built module had inserted itself into Mercury’s orbit, beginning a months-long series of manoeuvres. In the coming weeks, its two scientific probes — one built by ESA and the other by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — will separate, allowing each to follow its own orbit at a different altitude.

En route to Mercury the craft was able to test some of its onboard instruments. Mission scientists pointed the onboard X-ray camera, the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), at the Crab Nebula, the remnants of a supernova witnessed on Earth in 1054. MIXS is the first X-ray imaging device to be sent on an interplanetary mission, notes Emma Bunce, a plasma physicist at the University of Leicester, UK, who is one of BepiColombo’s leading mission scientists.

For the time being, the two probes will remain conjoined, until they reach the prescribed orbit for the JAXA probe, called MIO, on 9 December. It will trace ellipses at altitudes between 500 km and 11,000 km, sampling the planet’s magnetic field and how it interacts with solar wind. The ESA-built probe, which is called Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and carries MIXS, among other instruments, will then gradually descend until March 2027, when it will reach its orbit at between 400–1,500 km. From there, its instruments will continuously study the planet’s surface.

The BepiColumbo spacecraft (illustration).Credit: ESA - P. Carril.

Industry observers note that travelling to the Solar System’s innermost regions is a “prolonged affair”, Bunce says. “Energetically, it takes more energy to go to Mercury than to go to the outer Solar System,” says Bunce. BepiColombo debuted in October 2018, and needed to gradually lower itself closer to the Sun without gaining speed and overshooting Mercury.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall.
  • The satellite that launched with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 22, 1989, the space shuttle Discovery introduced on the secret mission STS-33 for the U.S. military. It lifted off from Kennedy Space Center and up into the dark of night.

This was the third nighttime launch of the shuttle program and the 32nd shuttle mission overall. Discovery had five astronauts on board. Their mission was to deploy a classified payload for the U.S. Department of Defense. NASA and the military rolled out several secretive shuttle missions to deploy military satellites.

The satellite that launched with STS-33 is believed to be a type of spy satellite called Magnum. But exactly what Magnum was doing in orbit remains classified.

Industry observers note that from its start, the Space Transportation System, better known as the space shuttle, was a compromise between meeting civilian and military needs. NASA saw the vehicle as a means of supporting science research, establishing an on-orbit economy (servicing commercial satellites and flying tech giant payloads) and ultimately, assembling the parts for a space station.

According to recent reports, the Department of Defense saw the shuttle as an asset to deploying and retrieving reconnaissance satellites, among other projects, some of them classified. It was not until the loss of the space shuttle Challenger, that it was decided that the shuttle would only be used by the military when it was key to national security. Other needs would be met by expendable launch vehicles (ELVs).As an aside, the STS-33 astronauts also spent Thanksgiving in space during this mission. But the holiday was off to a crappy start when the shuttle's toilet broke first thing in the morning. After spending most of the day fixing it, they got to enjoy their Thanksgiving turkey together.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

Hims & Hers rolls out newly introduced peptide treatments — while admitting there's more to learn about efficacy

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hims & Hers Health on Wednesday remarked it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S.
  • Even as it declared the upcoming products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.
  • According to recent reports, the newly introduced offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hims & Hers Health on Wednesday remarked it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S. as part of the initial rollout of its Peptides+ platform, all of which are not approved by regulators.

Even as it declared the upcoming products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.

According to recent reports, the newly introduced offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids. Those products have exploded in popularity among fitness and longevity enthusiasts who attest that they help with muscle growth, rapid injury recovery and anti-aging, even though most lack evidence from robust human trials.

Hims in late October launched an early access list for the upcoming peptide offerings, and more than 10,000 people signed up within 15 days, a manufacturer spokesperson noted in a statement.

It has been revealed that none of the tech giant's specific compounded products are approved by the Food and Drug Administration. But Hims mentioned they are authorized by law and formulated by pharmacies "that adhere to rigorous quality standards and are licensed and inspected by state boards of pharmacy.".

The products include compounded formulations of sermorelin, a peptide that stimulates growth-hormone release and is marketed for recovery, body composition and anti-aging; glutathione, a peptide promoted ‌for anti-aging and athletic recovery; and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NAD+, a coenzyme that plays a role in cellular metabolism.

Recent findings suggest that the company will also offer compounded versions of vitamin B-12, a vitamin needed to make red blood cells, build DNA, and maintain healthy nerve function, and L-carnitine, an amino acid derivative that helps the body turn fat into energy. The FDA has approved certain prescription forms of both peptides for established medical uses, primarily for diagnosed deficiencies in those compounds.

Hims noted it intends to add more peptides and therapies made in the U.S. over time. That includes BPC-157, an unapproved peptide derived from a protein found in human gastric juice that is marketed for healing processes. The organization also aims to introduce another unapproved peptide called TB-500, which is derived from a naturally occurring protein in the body and is marketed for broader, systemic soft-tissue recovery and flexibility. Most of the research on both has been conducted in animals, not humans.

To receive the products, members on the Hims platform will start with an assessment of health history and goals with a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies, who can tailor a personalized initiative to their needs, if appropriate.

The tech giant mentioned it intends to use its communication platform to check in with patients and ensure they are seeing desired results.

It has been revealed that "If they're not, we need to do something about it," Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, Hims chief medical officer, told CNBC. "We need to, you know, adjust the dose when that's appropriate, or in some cases consider other compounds that's maybe a better fit. And of course, there will also be cases when we need to refer people to other care options.".

However, Vinjamoori stated there's still uncertainty over how to best use the peptides.

According to recent reports, "We don't have all of this data that we're used to having with compounds like this," he mentioned. "We have the opportunity to get it right, and I think we see that as our responsibility with a firm of our size, our skill, and resources to really lead.".

Vinjamoori added that people who have serious illnesses, such as cardiovascular disease, liver disease and kidney disease, will not be candidates for the compounds for now.

Meanwhile, Andrew Huberman, a well known neuroscientist, podcaster and Stanford University School of Medicine professor who recently joined Hims' board of directors, in a statement called compounds "real medical treatments, not just a wellness trend." He noted Hims provides safe access through "trusted sourcing and physician oversight.".

But health experts raised concerns about the broader mainstream marketing of peptides in the U.S. and accessing them on telehealth platforms.

According to recent reports, "With peptides, I think you have to view them the same way you would view any drug that hasn't been rigorously tested," stated Joshua Kritzer, a chemistry professor at Tufts University. "Without actual testing, all you have is anecdotal information, and that's just not enough information to put a substance in your body.".

Kritzer said the lack of large clinical trials means researchers can't rule out potentially serious, rare complications from peptides — the kinds of risks that have led regulators to reject or pull otherwise effective drugs from the market after they underwent comprehensive testing in humans.

Without that testing, it's also unclear how telehealth firms, physicians and pharmacies can make decisions about what doses patients should take, said Paul Knoepfler, a cell biology and human anatomy professor at UC Davis Health. While some people rely on anecdotal data from real peptide consumers, "the dosing for these products really has not been established," he added.

Knoepfler said one risk is that injecting too much of a synthetic peptide into patients could trigger "weird immune responses that are really bad for one's health" because the body might recognize it as foreign.

"With the peptides, it's very loosey-goosey," Knoepfler told CNBC. "How does one even know what would be the effective amount for whatever you're hoping it will do, and what amount would have more risks?".

It has been revealed that but he mentioned the more contact patients can have with physicians around taking a compounded peptide, the better. Providers, including those tied to telehealth firms, should make sure patients are well-informed about the possible risks and unknowns of a given product and consider their preexisting conditions, cancer history and other medications, Knoepfler said.

That appears to be consistent with the approach Hims & Hers is taking. The tech giant states patients who use the peptide and longevity products can also use its Care+ offering, which pairs treatment with ongoing support. That includes twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress and the ability to message providers trained in peptide therapy around the clock with any questions.

Still, Kritzer argued that having a doctor who only knows a patient from online, essentially mail-order platforms or websites "is not enough supervision to put you on a prescription medication," especially an unapproved one.

Hims' ability to legally sell some of these peptides stems from a major shift in federal oversight by the Health and Human Services Department. It issued a policy in October that says the Food and Drug Administration will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or physicians that compound and dispense six unapproved peptides while formal rules are reviewed.

According to recent reports, in practice, that means these pharmacies and other firms can now offer them, even though the peptides aren't yet on the FDA's official list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make. It does not translate to formal approval of the specific peptides.

The policy followed a 2023 decision by the Biden administration where the FDA restricted compounding pharmacies from producing popular peptide formulations due to safety, impurity and immune-reaction concerns.

According to recent reports, HHS Secretary ​Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides, calling himself a "substantial fan" of the treatments and arguing that restrictions were driving Americans to potentially unsafe products from overseas. Kennedy has previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.

The announcement also comes after Hims in February 2025 acquired a California-based peptide manufacturing facility equipped with advanced peptide synthesizers.

The evidence for peptide efficacy varies by compound.

A 2026 systematic review screening 113 studies, including both small trials on humans along with rodent research, found zero eligible clinical outcome trials proving that administering IV or intramuscular NAD+ improves anti-aging, energy, or wellness endpoints in humans.

It has been revealed that there is some evidence for specific uses of certain peptides, such as potential weight loss. A review of 37 L-carnitine trials found participants lost about 2.7 pounds on average, though that analysis does not demonstrate that a compounded injection works the same way.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, vitamin B-12 injections are most commonly used to help people with a diagnosed deficiency rather than preventative care. U.S. survey data shows only 3.6% of adults are B-12 deficient.

In a recent development, glutathione's evidence is thin, too. IV injections of it are widely marketed for skin whitening, yet not FDA-approved for this purpose.

A small study published in the Journal of Pakistan Association of Dermatologists evaluating IV glutathione highlighted that the treatment is "not very effective" for skin-lightening, and that it loses efficacy with time.

The FDA also remarked in August that it received reports of at least 30 patients who experienced adverse events after they received compounded IV glutathione alone or in combination with other ingredients from different compounding pharmacies.

According to recent reports, all of the glutathione tied to the reports were from the same wholesale distributor and was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs. Two of the Texas pharmacies conducted recalls related to elevated endotoxin levels in their glutathione injectable drugs.

These studies and reports don't speak to how Hims' exact combination will perform, but they do highlight the current limits on data studying the treatments and the questions surrounding them.

Industry News: The Manosphere Isn’t Ready for Brothercore

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On a sweltering July morning, in the middle of an empty playground in suburban Denver, two extremely fit, sweaty, shirtless male influencers are tussling in the dirt.
  • According to recent reports, “The guy on top who’s in control, we call that position riding,” one of the grapplers, Carlos Monteon Jr.
  • Industry observers note that monteon and Cole continue scuffling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a sweltering July morning, in the middle of an empty playground in suburban Denver, two extremely fit, sweaty, shirtless male influencers are tussling in the dirt.

According to recent reports, “The guy on top who’s in control, we call that position riding,” one of the grapplers, Carlos Monteon Jr. pauses to explain to a group of eight similarly fit, sweaty, nearly all shirtless men who are watching the action in a circle. Monteon is a wrestler and influencer from Arizona, with pomelo-sized biceps, glossy shoulder-length hair, and more than 675,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram. He turns to his demo partner, Johnny Cole, a rangy, then 28-year-old content creator (59,000 TikTok followers) with a penchant for slutty tank tops. “And this one is called the Saturday night ride.”.

Industry observers note that monteon and Cole continue scuffling. The match ends with Monteon straddling Cole, their faces inches apart, their torsos glistening. The scene looks like a JV wrestling match.

The other men pair up to take turns grappling. Two cameramen circle them as a drone hums overhead.

“Yes, testosterone!” one influencer yells.

Recent findings suggest that “And estrogen!” Cole adds. “Both of them together, as one!”.

Sources indicate that I’m at Hey Brother House, a content incubator that hosts weeklong retreats for male social media influencers. The organization teaches men and boys “to embody healthy masculinity, fully process emotions, embrace authenticity, and show up as compassionate, empathetic community leaders,” according to its website.

Filmmaker Vince Nett captures the shirtless shenanigans of Carlos Monteon Jr.

Cole, the founder of Hey Brother, helms the project with two other house leaders. Jonathan Jacobs, an affable 37-year-old who owns a digital marketing agency in Los Angeles, is wearing a brown cap that says “Male Friendship.” Matthew Echelman, a 35-year-old Brooklyn-based filmmaker, has hired two crew members to film the whole thing for a possible future documentary. Funded by a grant of more than $180,000 from an initiative called the Young Men and Media Collective, Hey Brother House’s goal is to flood 18-to-25-year-old men’s social media feeds with content that will (hopefully) make them less terrible.

In a recent development, the house itself is a rented stucco McMansion next to the Green Valley Ranch Golf Club, a residential community just outside Denver. In some respects, it looks like your average fratty domicile: There’s a Nintendo Switch console in the living room, where the boys play Mario Kart; a basement decked out with fitness equipment, a sauna, air hockey, and Foosball; and a makeshift indoor putting green. But there’s also a strict house alcohol ban, remote-controlled bidets, a box of wigs, swag boxes filled with fuchsia “Redefining Masculinity” T-shirts, and a wall covered in Post-Its of “gifts” the men can give each other, including “laying down on couch or blanket in park with my head on your lap.” There’s even a room—the “Man Box”—for testimonials, where the “cast members” can speak directly to the camera about their day. It’s reminiscent of reality TV, except most everyone is aware of bell hooks’ All About Love: New Visions, and they are explicitly here to make friends.

These guys are all in Denver because, as Cole puts it while he smokes Marlboro Lights on the porch, “men and boys are not doing well. And they have not been doing well for a long time.” The evidence supporting this is manifold: Young men are less likely than their female counterparts to finish high school and then enroll in college. They’re dropping out of the job market, and they’re more likely to report loneliness and isolation, as well as more likely to die by suicide.

Part of the problem is the manosphere, the social media ecosystem populated by looksmaxxers, incels, AI-touting hustle bros, and peptide-injecting fitness influencers. Initially a relatively fringe coalition, the “manosphere” has evolved into an online force to be reckoned with, thanks to the massive success of influencers like Jordan Peterson, a former academic who has advocated for all-meat diets and climate-change denialism; and, later, Andrew Tate, a failed kickboxer turned minor webcam impresario, who is currently facing more than 40 criminal charges in the UK and Romania, including trafficking and sex crimes. By preaching traditional masculinity as a path toward self-empowerment, so-called manosphere influencers have appealed to an audience of young men disillusioned by the rise of identity politics. Social media algorithms have happily amplified that message: By 2023, clips featuring Tate had more than 13 billion views on social media platforms.

Left to right: Jonathan Jacobs, Chris Petrone, and Johnny Cole collaborate on a social media house-tour video.

It has been revealed that during the 2024 election, an estimated 67 percent of white male zoomers voted for Trump, resulting in a flurry of discourse about the manosphere’s power in channeling the frustrations of young men. “[They’ve] never had brotherhood or friendship,” Cole tells me. “They’ve never had another man look them in the eyes and say they’re worthy.” Men like Tate are successful, he says, because they “weaponize this insecurity and this fragility and give them a scapegoat and say, ‘If you buy my course and you learn how to drop-ship, or come to my alphas-only elite men's circle, then you’ll become a high-value man.’”.

In a recent development, of the three Hey Brother House leaders, Cole is the only one in the demographic the creators are trying to reach. He’s 6'4" and built like a varsity swimmer, with translucent green eyes, gray-painted nails, and light brown hair, which he dyes green and magenta for a short while after he leaves the house. He characterizes his work trying to reach young men as something akin to a divine calling.

It has been revealed that “I’m a white man who was a college rugby player, and I do jujitsu, but I also wear earrings and talk about feminism online,” he tells me. “Some of these guys think I’m performative, but in my experience, when I work with men and boys in person, they love me. They've never experienced a man who's a near peer who calls them into accountability, who offers them hugs and encouragement and support. In a looksmaxxing world, for these young guys I’m someone to look up to, literally and figuratively.”.

It has been revealed that this is where the Hey Brother House comes in: to teach progressive-leaning, male creators how to create content that captures the attention of the Kick-streaming, Zyn-sucking, butt-cut-sporting contingent. The goal is to adopt the visual hallmarks of the manosphere—slick editing, dynamic hooks, fast-paced montages—and apply those to what the house calls “healthy masculinity” content: dudes thrift-shopping together and picking out outfits, or guys playing golf while also wearing pink. “What we're not gonna do is stand in front of a camera, wag our fingers, and say, ‘I think that the patriarchy is the fucking worst thing in the world,’” Cole indicates.

Of course, there’s plenty of content for young men on social media that does not encourage men to become webcam pimps or forcefully hit themselves in the face with hammers, a la Clavicular. But much of the content in the “healthy masculinity” space is filled with academic jargon and feminist buzzwords. Or it’s more along the lines of Joe Rogan–infused, “Thunderdome-style” masculinity. (Think Instagram posts of white men with tribal tattoos weeping in the desert, with a caption promoting an online crypto investing class.) The Hey Brother House aims to teach male influencers how to promote values like empathy and vulnerability, via content about wrestling or fitness or style or financial advice. “It’s sugar with the medicine,” Cole says.

An activity at the Hey Brother House where members offer gifts to the group and request actions they would like to receive from others.

It has been revealed that in selecting the initial cohort for the Hey Brother House, Cole, Echelman, and Jacobs had to strike a delicate balance: They wanted creators who would be “mission-aligned,” as Jacobs put it, but who don’t exclusively make political content. Out of more than 130 applicants, they selected eight men. Some were leftist commentators like Jerry Zeng (133,000 Instagram followers), a 29-year-old, tatted, Jacquemus shorts-wearing video essayist from Houston, and Ian Lightfoot (1 million Instagram followers), an immaculately-eyebrowed, now 26-year-old whose Instagram bio proffers “positivity, popcorn, and bite-sized politics.” Others were more conventional lifestyle influencers like Sean Jones, a premed student who makes cute date-night videos and productivity vlogs, and the Houston-based trainer Stephen Marmolejos (180,000 TikTok followers), who posts fitness content and does sponcon for brands like Corona and Thayers. One, the artist and dancer Mars Wright (195,000 TikTok followers), is a trans man who has never lived in a house with cis men before. “I kind of feel like I’m entering the cafeteria scene in Mean Girls,” he told me before he got to Denver.

In a recent development, I arrive at the house from my hotel to find the guys midway through a vulnerability exercise in the living room. (For four days, I was given almost total access but was politely asked not to attend the first day of exercises, so the men could bond.).

I quietly take a seat on a corduroy couch as the men stand in two parallel lines, facing their partners and taking turns answering the question: “What would you know if you really knew me?” All speaking at once, they say things like: “my father,” “my angry feelings,” “even my best relationship,” “Weight Watchers.” They are mic’d, and the cameras are out in full force, zooming in as the men embrace and thank each other for listening. Some are crying.

Sources indicate that later, the guys sit in a talking circle—one of many I would witness—and unpack their feelings. This is the first time some of them, particularly the brawnier health-and-fitness influencer types, have had such intimate conversations with other men, talking about their marriages, surviving domestic violence, trauma, addiction. “I started out with vague surface-level things that were quirky,” Monteon indicates afterward, “but at the very end I felt safe enough, and I revealed way more than I expected to.”.

Cole, who leads the exercise, nods empathetically. “You can’t heal if you don’t reveal,” he claims, the men snapping in assent. (There is a lot of affirmative snapping at the house; there is also repeated use of terms like “aligned,” “affirmed,” and “container,” a reference to a therapeutic trauma-processing modality. I heard about containers a dozen times, only once in the context of a physical vessel.).

In a recent development, the next morning, when I meet the guys for the first full day’s activity—a trip to a thrift store where the men select outfits for each other—approximately 40 percent of them are hungover from karaoke the night before, as well as the day of emotional disclosures. (As Zeng put it to me, “there’s been a lot of trauma-dumping.”) But they seem genuinely psyched for the activity, which is intended to culminate in filming a wholesome “dress your bro for a night out”–type video.

Journaling is a popular practice at the Hey Brother House.

“It’s a lot of pressure. I’ve never shopped for another dude, [or] heard a man compliment another man’s outfit,” Chris Petrone (1.6 million TikTok followers), tells me. “At first I was nervous, but then I was like, let’s get funky.” A baby-faced 31-year-old who lives in Florida, Petrone is one of the most successful creators in the Hey Brother House, thanks in part to a 2021 viral video in which he advocated for men to stock tampons in their bathrooms for female guests; for about a year, he had “the CEO of tampons” in his bio.

According to recent reports, if they are nervous, they don’t show it. Monteon, who arrives in a Movember cap and brown sweats, leaves with jeans and a brown and white geometric-patterned button-down, looking like a 1970s Tiger Beat centerfold. And when Lightfoot tries on a purple and yellow cropped windbreaker, Wright and Josh Kennedy, a 29-year-old mustachioed, Wichita-based personal trainer, snap in assent. “That was literally made for you,” Kennedy states.

Recent findings suggest that the Hey Brother House was conceived, at least in part, as a content incubator. But aside from the documentary film crew being present for almost every activity, not a ton of content is actually being made. Occasionally, I turn a corner and see guys editing footage on a laptop or someone filming multiple takes of a house tour in the foyer.

It has been revealed that instead, the dudes seemed focused on … being dudes. They played Mario Kart and went for runs. They talked about what dog breeds they would be. “I am not a scary dog,” Jones said. “And I do believe I am majestic at times.”.

Even Wright, who was initially anxious about living in a house with cis men—some of whom had never met a trans man before—swiftly bonded with the other members. “I've always wanted to be in community with other men and feel like I belonged and like I was one of them,” he says. “And honestly, I didn’t really believe that a lot of men were having these conversations until I was behind closed doors with them.”.

Industry observers note that the bros are sitting in the living room for a content brainstorming session. They are watching a slew of manosphere clips, which Cole notes embody the three “Rs” of masculinity: “relentlessly rich and ripped.” He then demonstrates a few examples of Reels that he identifies as “really brother-core coded”: a challenge video of men guessing the drinks that have been thrown in their faces, or tips for how men can protect their girlfriends from drink-spiking at bars. The goal, says Jacobs, is not to “attack the messenger” by making fun of Andrew Tate or Jordan Peterson because “that puts people on the defensive.” The men volley around a few ideas, which are similarly wholesome and tongue-in-cheek: golf cart racing, a parody of Jordan Peterson, rating each other’s hugs.

Sources indicate that then Wright pitches an idea for an “ask a trans person” video series, and the warm brotherly vibes start to shift. Wright prefaces his pitch by saying that, during his time in the house, a few of the other members had unintentionally “asked him questions that you should never ask a trans person.” Though he doesn’t name names or call anyone out specifically, he proposes that the snafu serves as a teaching moment for cisgender men watching Hey Brother House content.

Recent findings suggest that “Trans people don’t believe that any cis men care about them at all,” Wright indicates. “I want to show my community that there are men who care for them and would stand up for them and would be willing to be put in a situation that makes them a little uncomfortable.”.

Many of the guys are on board, but Cole visibly bristles at the suggestion, saying the idea causes him “reservation [and] anxiety” due to the possibility of it generating backlash from LGBTQ viewers.

According to recent reports, the group holds a meeting to talk through a conflict that has caused tension. Facing camera, left to right: Chris Petrone and Johnny Cole. Facing away, from left to right: Ian Lightfoot and Jerry Zeng.

In a recent development, “I wasn’t worried about being canceled,” he tells me later. “I was worried about the emotional and energetic impact of that series when we, as a container of men, had not addressed the emotional and energetic impact of things that had been said offline.” But this wasn’t how Wright interpreted it. “I was really shocked he reacted like that,” he says. “He’s one of the few cis men to say that trans people really belong, and he invited me here, which was a dream come true. And it’s so gut-wrenchingly painful to see somebody react to you like, ‘Well, I don’t know how this is going to make me look.’”.

The impact of the conflict doesn’t become clear until the next day, when members of the House are abruptly summoned upstairs for a “tribunal.”.

It has been revealed that the vibes are off almost immediately. The House members clearly have no idea what the purpose of the meeting is and are even more flummoxed when one of the camera crew members asks them to head back down and come up again, so they can get a better take. They sit in a circle, baffled, as Echelman, not Cole, opens the meeting by reading a seven-minute statement off his iPhone. Echelman, the documentarian, has largely been absent from the House activities. He occasionally chimes in during meetings and with video pitches during the brainstorm, including “a haunted house, but the ghosts are subverting gender expectations.”.

“In line with safety and consent, some things have arisen over the course of the house around conflict that I think it's crucial to not shy away from, but welcome and embrace and talk through,” he reads. “Rather than let that pass quietly, we want to name how we hold conflict here. Conflict isn't a failure of this space. It's where we practice communication, accountability, and care. And holding space means letting someone name their experience without filtering it.” Then Echelman opens the floor for questions.

On the third floor, the day after the tense emotional group meeting, all that remains is a box of tissues.

Immediately, someone says that they’re confused. “I echo that sentiment,” Cole says. “Are there things that you would like to name that you have observed in this space which prompted you to write that and call this meeting?”.

Industry observers note that echelman’s explanation lasts an additional five minutes, over the course of which two things gradually become clear to everyone present: (1) this meeting is about Cole, and (2) he had no idea. Echelman accuses Cole of unintentionally abusing his leadership position to shut people down, and he brings up a critique raised by one house member that the “dress your bro” thrifting activity could be perceived on social media as “poverty porn” or depriving resources from low-income communities. (Echelman’s own “haunted house for toxic masculinity” pitch is not specifically mentioned.) “In a leadership position, it's our responsibility to, even if we’re feeling something in the moment, not to make it about us but someone else being so vulnerable and opening up to us,” he says.

It has been revealed that the tribunal, several house members told me afterward, was a disaster. As the men splinter off to go rock-climbing or golfing, Lightfoot tells me, “It felt less like an authentic conversation and more like a reality TV show.” A visibly upset Wright notes he had confronted Cole privately about the brainstorm and specifically told Echelman that he did not want to have a meeting in front of the cameras with the group about what happened. To hear him tell it, he was less angry than disappointed. “Their hearts are in the right place,” he says of the House leaders. “They’re working tooth and nail, day and night, to make a difference. But we’re still so far from where we need to be.”.

Later, Echelman will dispute others’ characterization of the tribunal: “Plenty of people after the conversation remarked that we broke the glass ceiling, because we could finally be open and honest with one another,” he tells me later.

Recent findings suggest that he isn’t entirely wrong. After the initial confrontation with Cole, some of the men brought up their own minor conflicts from Hey Brother House. Without exception, they had been addressed graciously and without grandstanding. There was no bluster for the cameras, no aggression, no dick-measuring; none of what you would come to expect from a group of men in conflict with each other. They listened. They affirmed. They told each other how grateful they were for the experience of being there together. Even if the house leaders were in conflict, the creators themselves were “synced up completely,” Wright tells me. “I look at any one of them, and I know they would make me feel safe and comfortable.” It didn’t necessarily make for compelling content, but it did seem like they had taken Cole’s earlier lesson to heart: you can’t heal if you don’t reveal. (Snaps).

Josh Kennedy (left) and Johnny Cole have a heartfelt conversation while doing the dishes.

In a recent development, cole, Echelman, and Jacobs are now selecting the cohort for the next House, which will take place in Austin in December, followed by a third in Atlanta. Nearly all eight are already confirmed, including leftist bodybuilder Colin Davis and trans former NCAA athlete Schuyler Bailar. The leaders have apparently hashed things out and are working to correct some of the mistakes they made with the Denver House, enlisting the services of an in-person, trained men’s group facilitator to mediate conflicts. “This is a test-and-learn pilot,” Jacobs tells me. “While we are comfortable with swings and misses, we also want to ensure we don’t keep taking the same swing.” Cole’s friend, whom he describes as a “professional race car driver and videographer,” will also be on hand to record social media content. “He's 22 and has a really vibey aesthetic,” he says. “He knows what's t-u-f-f, tuff.”.

Sources indicate that all told, the creators at the Hey Brother House produced somewhere between 65 and 70 videos. The main focus was on bonding activities and group discussions. The highest-performing video was a clip of Wright injecting himself with testosterone as the other men cheered him on, which got 689,000 views. After the tribunal, the House also produced his “Ask a Trans Man” video series, which overperformed on both Instagram and Wright’s YouTube channel; in one, Cole and Wright, who have since made up, were prominently featured.

Little of the content from Hey Brother House went viral, but for a handful of the creators, their audience now skews more male; Wright, for instance, notes some of his content from the house reached a predominantly male audience. But in reaching their target demo—men from 18 to 25—they saw little success. “There are some ways in which our content was too on the nose,” says Cole. In the future, he says they’ll make more of “the type of stuff that young men want to see” — such as the wrestling videos, which he says overperformed. For this reason, they’re trying to recruit a much younger cohort for Austin, who focus less on political commentary and more on skits and lifestyle content. They’re having some difficulty: many younger male creators often have to juggle their content creation with school. A lot of them have talent managers who don’t want their clients to “get too political,” or have turned down the House because they can’t pay them that much.

Josh Kennedy (left) cheers on Johnny Cole and Ian Lightfoot as they hug after their dance-off performances at The Movement Project.

But there are signs pointing in the direction of a healthier version of manhood being promoted on social media—or, at the very least, an exhaustion with older models. Following the midterm elections in November, men like senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed, James Talarico, and Sen. Jon Ossoff emerged triumphant at the polls, proffering a kindler and gentler (not to mention hunkier) model of masculinity than any proffered by a Clavicular or an Androgenic. Perhaps even more tellingly, white men between the ages of 18 and 29, who had previously helped deliver the 2024 election to Trump, swung overwhelmingly left. According to one analysis, 54 percent of this bracket voted for Democratic House candidates.

Recent findings suggest that there was also one video that came out of Denver that did indeed perform well with the target demographic of Gen Z men. A simple, five-second looping Instagram Reel highlights Kennedy and Cole locked in an embrace. “When’s the last time you got a hug longer than 5 seconds?” the onscreen text reads. It has garnered 500,000 views, mostly from 18-to-24-year-olds.

Sources indicate that I am reminded of something Cole told me the first time we spoke about how to solve the toxic masculinity crisis. “I know so strongly in my soul that more men and boys just need more hugs,” he said. “No matter what you’ve been through, no matter who you are. You just need more hugs [and] safe touches and affirmation and encouragement.” At the time, this struck me as cringe, and maybe a bit too simplistic. Watching the Reel with Kennedy and Cole embracing, I feel the same. But that doesn’t mean it’s not also true.

Ford starts U.S. battery cell production using Chinese tech amid geopolitical tensions

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, MARSHALL, Mich.
  • Industry observers note that the automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out.
  • The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

Industry observers note that the automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.

Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible.

"If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke remarked Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells.".

Industry observers note that the U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

Industry observers note that ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

In a recent development, ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.

Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.

The facility is highly automated, but Ford mentioned it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it intends to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

#59045. Latest Update: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1000 w)
📖 Baca

Latest Update: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A bizarre prehistoric whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so crooked that researchers initially suspected its fossilized skull had been distorted after death.
  • According to recent reports, sperm whales and pygmy sperm whales are already known for having some of the strangest head shapes among mammals.
  • Now, an international team of scientists has identified an extinct pygmy sperm whale species that took this unusual anatomy to an entirely new level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A bizarre prehistoric whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so crooked that researchers initially suspected its fossilized skull had been distorted after death. Instead, its extraordinary shape was completely natural and may represent the most extreme facial asymmetry ever documented in a mammal.

According to recent reports, sperm whales and pygmy sperm whales are already known for having some of the strangest head shapes among mammals. While most vertebrates have bodies and skulls that are roughly symmetrical on both sides, toothed whales have evolved uneven skull structures to accommodate specialized organs responsible for producing sound and navigating through echolocation.

Now, an international team of scientists has identified an extinct pygmy sperm whale species that took this unusual anatomy to an entirely new level. Named Scaphokogia huachafo, the whale lived during the Late Miocene, between 6.3 and 5.6 million years ago, and measured approximately 2.7 meters in length. Its fossilized skull displays the most extreme facial asymmetry known in any whale or dolphin, and possibly in any mammal.

A Prehistoric Whale With an Extraordinary Skull.

"Cranial asymmetry in toothed whales is directly linked to the development of fatty structures in the forehead that are involved in sound production. But in Scaphokogia huachafo, this asymmetry went far beyond the area around the blowhole. Both bony nostrils are shifted entirely to the left side of the skull, while the facial bones differ dramatically in size and position. The skull looks completely crooked," explains Aldo Benites-Palomino, lead author of the study.

It has been revealed that benites-Palomino investigated the fossil during his doctoral research at the University of Zurich's Department of Paleontology. He is currently an assistant professor at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU).

In a recent development, the whale's extraordinary appearance also inspired its scientific name. The word huachafo comes from Peruvian Spanish and is commonly used to describe something excessively flashy, bizarre, extravagant, or even tacky.

"In Peru, huachafo is an everyday word for anything that is flashy, over-the-top, bizarre, extravagant or difficult to categorize aesthetically," claims Benites-Palomino.

"When we looked at the proportions of this whale - with its face strongly shifted to the left and its oversized, downward-curving snout - it broke every rule of symmetry and elegance seen in living cetaceans. Its anatomy is so extravagant and odd that huachafo seemed the perfect name for it.".

Scientists Initially Suspected the Skull Was Deformed.

Sources indicate that the remarkable fossil was originally recovered during the mid-1990s from the Pisco Formation in southern Peru. This desert region is famous among paleontologists for its exceptionally preserved fossils of ancient marine animals.

In a recent development, benites-Palomino first encountered the specimen in 2015 while preparing his Bachelor's thesis at the Museo de Historia Natural in Lima. Its dramatically uneven shape immediately raised an vital question: Was the skull genuinely this crooked when the whale was alive, or had millions of years of geological pressure distorted it?

"The initial suspicion with skulls this distorted is always taphonomy - that the specimen may have been flattened or twisted by sediment pressure over millions of years," indicates Benites-Palomino.

"But the sutures are fully closed, and there are no fractures, pathologies or deformations elsewhere on the skull. This was genuine biology, not a result of poor preservation.".

The findings confirmed that the extraordinary asymmetry was part of the whale's natural anatomy, rather than damage caused by burial, fossilization, or disease.

A Bizarre Adaptation for Hunting Along the Seafloor.

Sources indicate that the whale's unusual skull also offers clues about how it survived. Modern sperm whales typically pursue squid in deep ocean waters, but Scaphokogia huachafo appears to have followed a very different hunting strategy. Its anatomy suggests that it was highly adapted to searching for food along the bottom of shallow coastal waters.

One of its most distinctive features was a large, tube-shaped snout strengthened by dense bone and cartilage that had hardened into bone. These heavy structures served as natural ballast, moving the whale's center of gravity forward and downward.

Its snout also pointed downward at an angle of 31 degrees relative to the rest of its skull. By reconstructing the joint connecting the skull to the first neck vertebra, known as the atlas, scientists determined that Scaphokogia could bend its head downward by as much as 55 degrees.

"The entire cranio-cervical complex is modified to point the snout directly toward the bottom," explains Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, co-author of the study and doctoral advisor at the University of Zurich.

"The combination of dense bone, the downward-curving snout and the flexible neck articulation allowed the animal to move directly above the seabed and feed close to the sediment.".

It has been revealed that researchers also believe the whale may have relied on its highly specialized echolocation system to locate prey beneath the soft sediment of coastal environments. Unlike other marine mammals that forage along the ocean floor, Scaphokogia lacked the sensitive facial whiskers or specialized visual adaptations that can help animals find food near the bottom.

Instead, its extraordinarily asymmetrical skull may have supported a sophisticated biological sonar system that allowed it to detect hidden prey.

This unusual feeding strategy represents a specialized way of life that no longer exists among modern marine mammals. As ocean conditions shifted toward the end of the Miocene, the ecological niche occupied by Scaphokogia disappeared, eventually giving way to the marine mammal communities familiar today.

The discovery provides a remarkable glimpse into how far evolution once pushed the anatomy of whales, producing a creature whose dramatically crooked face was not a deformity, but an adaptation to a vanished underwater world.
