📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget intends by former Prime Minister Liz Truss. Now, it’s enjoying a comeback.

It has been revealed that sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022. The pound, which has advanced about 3.3% versus the greenback since the start of 2023, is the best-performing currency among developed economies this year.

Recent findings suggest that the UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected. Activity is now thought to have expanded 0.1% in the final three months of last year, up from a previous estimate of no growth at all. Gross domestic product growth in January has been estimated at 0.3% after dropping 0.5% in December.

This resilience is bolstering expectations the Bank of England will maintain aggressive interest rate hikes despite concerns about the health of the global banking sector. Rising rates can boost the domestic currency because they help attract foreign investors searching for higher returns.

Inflation in the United Kingdom also jumped to an annual rate of 10.4% in February, underscoring the need for the Bank of England to maintain its tough approach.

The pound plunged close to $1.03 in September 2022 after the Truss government unveiled intends to boost borrowing while slashing taxes, unleashing panic in financial markets that fueled fears of a recession in the United Kingdom.

The International Monetary Fund predicted in January that the UK economy would contract by 0.6% this year, while all other advanced economies would grow, if only slightly.

“There was a lot of pessimism being priced into the pound,” noted Francesco Pesole, a currency strategist at ING.

But the sharp pullback in energy prices and China’s reopening have provided some relief about the economic outlook since the start of the year.

“There was a substantial re-rating of growth expectations around Europe, and that impacted the UK,” Pesole stated.

Sources indicate that the euro has also been lifted by these dynamics, rising 2.3% against the US dollar in 2023. The pound’s rally has been sharper in large part because its 2022 declines were more severe, according to Pesole.

Both currencies have been aided by the greenback’s sharp drop from highs reached last September as recession fears have percolated in the United States.

Industry observers note that A lack of clarity around the Federal Reserve’s next steps has also restrained the dollar in recent weeks. Investor speculation has increased that the Fed could pause or stop rate hikes due to concerns about the economy following the failure of Silicon Valley Bank last month.

Jordan Rochester, a currency strategist at Nomura, said he thinks the pound could rise to $1.30 this year and “potentially higher.” But he still sees risks given the uncertainty surrounding the Bank of England’s plans and how rate rises will feed back through the country’s economy. And Pesole cautioned that currency fluctuations are often overdone when markets are choppy, as they are now.

“In a volatile market environment, moves are exacerbated,” he said.

Tech Report: NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Communications Lead for the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer.
  • An international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before.
  • Using 15 years of data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Communications Lead for the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer.

An international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before. This opens the door to discovering many more of these rapidly spinning objects. A paper describing the results published Thursday in the Physical Review Letters.

Using 15 years of data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor.

By comparison, the previous best method failed to find the pulsar, despite using enough computing power that a standard processor would take 600 years to perform the calculation.

In a recent development, A pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radiation toward Earth, much like a lighthouse. Finding pulsars in gamma-ray data is extraordinarily difficult because Fermi detects only a tiny number of photons from a given pulsar, mixed in with background noise from other gamma-ray-emitting sources and the broader universe. To find the signal, researchers must accurately guess several unknowns at once: how fast the star spins, how quickly the spin is slowing down, and precisely where it sits in the sky. Searching every possible combination would require an impossible number of computations.

According to recent reports, "We don't see every rotation from the pulsar, and we can't just count the rotations to work out where the photon came from," said lead author Daniel Pook-Kolb, a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics (Albert Einstein Institute) in Germany. “We have a four-dimensional grid, and we must search each direction with millions of trials in it. There’s just not enough computing power on Earth to do it.”.

Recent findings suggest that traditionally, scientists have searched for these pulsars by breaking Fermi data into smaller chunks and analyzing them by crowdsourcing computing power from volunteers around the world. Even with these volunteers contributing their computers’ unused processing power to run searches, it typically took the equivalent of hundreds of computer-years to identify a single pulsar.

Gazith and Zackay realized that the search could be transformed into a geometry problem: finding the shortest vector in a high-dimensional lattice, or a regularly spaced array of points. This lattice technique draws on algorithms developed by cryptographers trying to break encryption systems designed to resist code-breaking by future quantum computers. The method has also been used to help make satellite navigation systems more efficient.

"We have nothing to do with cryptography in our analysis here, but those algorithms can help us solve the problem of searching for pulsars in our data," Gazith said.

According to recent reports, each trial run of the algorithm took about five minutes on a single computer core — easily doable on a standard laptop, which usually has between two and eight cores. Once the lattice method identified a pulsar candidate, the researchers confirmed it by feeding in the full Fermi data set, revealing a signal so strong it could not be a chance occurrence.

Recent findings suggest that the team’s next goal is even more ambitious: finding pulsars in binary systems, where a pulsar orbits a star. These discoveries have long been considered out of reach because a companion star’s gravity distorts the signal in ways that have made these pulsars essentially impossible to discover with traditional methods.

In a recent development, "We know that there are probably tens or maybe even hundreds of these pulsars in the data set that we just couldn't find," said Colin Clark, an astrophysicist at the Max Planck Institute who co-authored the study. "The next goal is to extend the searches and use the combination of the new algorithm and the crowdsourced computing power from volunteers in our Einstein@Home program to hopefully find many new pulsars that we think should be there.”.

The discovery would not have happened without NASA's longstanding, Gold Standard Science policy of making its science data, including data from Fermi, freely available to anyone. Released in 2008, Fermi surveys the entire sky every three hours, observing the universe in gamma rays — the highest-energy form of light. After an initial one-year calibration period, all Fermi data became fully public and continues to be released as soon as it is processed.

Sources indicate that "The nice thing about NASA data is it's all open," Clark remarked. "All 18 years of Fermi data have been made public, and the data just keeps growing.".

That openness allowed researchers from outside the Fermi mission, including the cryptography-inspired team, to apply a completely new approach to the dataset. NASA’s support for the science community, through open software and tools such as NASA's Fermitools, enabled the team to prepare their dataset before beginning their analysis.

The Fermi mission has grown its catalog from a few hundred gamma ray sources to thousands, with newly introduced findings emerging as scientists apply fresh ideas to the same data.

Recent findings suggest that "Any search that one team is doing, another team can just go and do that and check the search," noted Elizabeth Hays, Fermi project scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "It's made all of the science better.".

#59042. A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (742 w)

A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A century after the Taung Child transformed our understanding of where humans came from, scientists are discovering that this famous fossil still has surprises to reveal.
  • The international study was led by Professor Gabriele Macho of the Archaeology, Environmental Changes and Geo-Chemistry (AMGC) research group at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB).
  • First discovered in South Africa in 1924, the Taung Child provided the first concrete evidence supporting the African origins of humanity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A century after the Taung Child transformed our understanding of where humans came from, scientists are discovering that this famous fossil still has surprises to reveal. A newly introduced study published in Nature dates the ancient remains to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years ago and suggests that the human family tree in southern Africa was much more complicated than previously believed.

The international study was led by Professor Gabriele Macho of the Archaeology, Environmental Changes and Geo-Chemistry (AMGC) research group at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB). The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how early human relatives evolved and how different species were related.

First discovered in South Africa in 1924, the Taung Child provided the first concrete evidence supporting the African origins of humanity. It also became the original "type specimen" used to define the species Australopithecus africanus. However, scientists never established definitive criteria for assigning later fossil discoveries to this species. As a result, the Taung Child remains the only fossil that can be identified with certainty as Australopithecus africanus.

According to recent reports, "For over 100 years, we assumed the Taung Child was just one of many similar fossils from the era," indicates Professor Gabriele Macho. "Our findings turn that on its head. The human family tree wasn't a neat, straight trunk -- it was a chaotic, tangled bush driven by climate shifts.".

Ancient Fossils Reveal a More Complex Human Family Tree.

It has been revealed that to investigate how the Taung Child compared with other early human relatives, researchers examined tooth structure and patterns of brain and dental development during growth. They found that several adult fossils traditionally classified as Australopithecus africanus followed developmental patterns that differed from those of the Taung Child.

Differences in brain development were particularly revealing. They suggest that fossils previously grouped into a single species may actually represent several distinct hominin species that inhabited the Sterkfontein region, either at the same time or during different periods.

These findings raise vital questions about the diversity of our ancient ancestors and suggest that early human evolution followed a much more complicated path than scientists once assumed.

How Climate Change Shaped Human Evolution.

Industry observers note that the researchers believe that dramatic environmental changes played a major role in creating this evolutionary diversity. Millions of years ago, southern Africa experienced repeated shifts between wetter and drier climates, continually transforming the landscape and the habitats available to early human relatives.

As suitable environments expanded and contracted, ancient hominin populations moved with them. Some groups became geographically isolated and evolved along different paths, while others eventually came back into contact and interbred. These changing conditions also exposed populations to different predators and pathogens, creating additional pressures that shaped their evolution.

Southern Africa's position along the boundary between tropical and temperate ecosystems made it especially notable in this process. Over thousands of years, shifting habitats may have repeatedly brought different hominin species together, creating opportunities for interbreeding and hybridization.

A Greener South Africa 3 Million Years Ago.

Industry observers note that the study also reveals a surprising picture of the environment in which the Taung Child lived. Evidence preserved in fossilized pollen indicates that the region was once considerably wetter and more heavily forested than it is today.

Researchers identified evidence of tree species that are now found hundreds of kilometers to the northeast, suggesting that the landscape surrounding the Taung Child was dramatically different from modern South Africa.

It has been revealed that together, these discoveries challenge the traditional view of human evolution as a relatively straightforward progression from one species to another. Instead, they point to a shifting network of populations that repeatedly separated, adapted, reunited, and sometimes interbred as environmental conditions changed.

In a recent development, more than 100 years after its discovery, the Taung Child is once again transforming our understanding of human origins. Its latest secrets suggest that the emergence of our own genus, Homo, was preceded by a far more diverse and interconnected world of ancient human relatives than previously recognized.

Latest Update: Experts say ‘trusted messengers’ critical as Amish grapple with measles outbreak

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unfolding crisis reveals importance of ‘human connections’ over the long term – especially in under-vaccinated areas.
  • Recent findings suggest that tristan Sharratt, a family nurse practitioner and public health researcher, began serving an Amish community in central New York almost inadvertently.
  • In a recent development, he is what is called a “trusted messenger” – someone who understands a community and has earned their respect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unfolding crisis reveals importance of ‘human connections’ over the long term – especially in under-vaccinated areas.

Recent findings suggest that tristan Sharratt, a family nurse practitioner and public health researcher, began serving an Amish community in central New York almost inadvertently. A friend told an Amish neighbor that Sharratt was accepting new patients and was a good, solid guy. Word spread rapidly, and now Sharratt sees many members of the community, which numbers in the hundreds.

In a recent development, he is what is called a “trusted messenger” – someone who understands a community and has earned their respect. Other trusted messengers can be neighbors, co-workers, customers, midwives, or people who work as long-distance drivers for the Amish. Connecting with such people will be crucial for ending the measles outbreak and preventing future crises.

“We can’t build trust with these communities just dropping in and being like, ‘Hey, there’s a measles outbreak. You should get vaccinated.’ Trust-building with these communities takes months to years,” Sharratt said. “This is a hard lesson and a tremendous opportunity to start building connections with these communities, because that is what it’s going to take to prevent the next situation like this.”.

The unfolding measles outbreak, which has killed at least eight people in Pennsylvania, two in Wisconsin, one in Upcoming York, and one in Virginia, also demonstrates the importance of funding public health long-term – for everything from water fluoridation to road safety, noted Sharratt, who is also a clinical lecturer of nursing and public health at Binghamton University.

“There’s just this enormous amount of work to be done,” he remarked.

Measles has raged through communities of Plain Anabaptists – including Amish and Mennonites – in this and previous outbreaks, and they are “emblematic” of many rural communities that have not been reached well by public health, Sharratt noted.

“We haven’t invested in rural communities in a long time from a public health perspective,” Sharratt stated, “and we’re really seeing the consequences with this outbreak.”.

In a recent development, A central belief for the Amish is Gelassenheit, which essentially means “God’s will” – the idea that one’s life belongs to God; both joy and suffering are God’s will. “Part of my conversations with them is trying to determine why scientific advancements don’t fit into the perspective of God’s will,” Sharratt remarked. “Why is it not God’s will that scientists have developed the technology to [prevent measles]?”.

Being unvaccinated in Plain Anabaptist communities is usually “an outcome of this whole idea of plain living”, Sharratt stated. But the work of anti-vaccine activists accelerated alongside the Covid pandemic, and “unfortunately it has started to creep in” to Amish communities as well, Sharratt said. Non-Amish anti-vaccine groups such as Children’s Health Defense – then led by Robert F Kennedy Jr, now the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services – held events and wrote articles for Plain Anabaptist publications, overtly targeting the communities with vaccine misinformation.

Amish life centers around community, and so should efforts to reach them.

“Human connection really should be at the center,” Sharratt noted. “You really just have to approach these people as people, build relationships as peers first, and then be there when they’re ready to talk to you or ask your opinion about these health issues.”.

Inroads to Amish communities are frequently informal. “Maybe the associate public health director just happens to drive by the Amish farm every day and buy something from the vegetable stand – it can be as simple as that,” Sharratt mentioned. Business owners and contractors can be a good way to connect.

According to recent reports, “The Amish will work as subcontractors, and then all of a sudden you’re working next to Amos on the build site, and you’re there for eight hours together doing rough carpentry, and you have the chance to talk,” he said. “Maybe you go to an Amish family’s bake stand every Saturday to get the pie, and you just happen to run into them and build a relationship.”.

There are local health departments that have done a great job of building connections – Sharratt pointed to the Otsego county health department, which developed a strong relationship with two Amish communities two decades ago during a pertussis outbreak; they continue to run vaccine clinics three to four times a year with those communities.

Often, however, health departments might know where a Plain Anabaptist community is, but they might not know how many people live there, how many children there are, or what the vaccination rate is.

“We have a huge data problem with these communities,” Sharratt said. “That requires going back to old methods of epidemiology, of community public health.” And public health at the national and state level hasn’t been as focused on community-building, he said.

According to recent reports, many Amish people want access to modern medicine when they need it – but access is frequently a challenge. Most Amish communities participate in some version of community insurance, where everyone chips in to cover healthcare costs. But typically providers accept conventional insurance; even those who negotiate lower prices with uninsured patients may be cost-prohibitive – especially as medicine is more corporatized and profit-driven, Sharratt said. That means communities often end up with providers who may not be as locked into conventional medicine.

Sources indicate that it’s notable to note that one Amish community is one Amish community; each makes unique decisions about healthcare, he said. “It’s not as simple as saying, ‘OK, here’s the strategy for all Amish communities in New York state.’ You need to approach every single one as a unique entity.” And there may be variability even within the communities, with some families seeking out vaccines despite anti-vax perspectives from community leaders.

According to recent reports, A strong focus on community can also be an asset. “Once you convince [Amish] communities to adopt a certain intervention or vaccination or something, it’s likely that you will get buy-in from more than just a couple of families. The reward for the work is, I think, relatively higher than [other] rural communities,” Sharratt said. Infectious diseases may spread rapidly, but so does trust once it takes root.

It has been revealed that “We can change it,” Sharratt noted of the course of the outbreak. “We definitely can. It’s just going to take a change in how we’re approaching these things.”.
